articles.title_orig: Germany’s telescoping wind turbine becomes world’s tallest
articles.title_zh: Germany’s telescoping wind turbine becomes world’s tallest
articles.content_orig:
Germany is taking wind power to new heights with a turbine almost as tall as Berlin’s iconic television tower at Alexanderplatz. Standing 365 m (1,198 ft) in Schipkau, the new world’s tallest wind turbine aims to tap stronger, steadier winds and test whether existing wind farms could gain a second story.
Built by engineering company Gicon for Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation, SPRIND, the pilot explores a way to generate more electricity from sites already devoted to wind power.
Gicon’s turbine stands about 25 m (82 ft) taller than Dongfang Electric’s 26-MW prototype in China, a machine designed for offshore use but installed at an onshore testing site. However, height and rated generating capacity are different contests. Offshore turbines typically benefit from stronger, less turbulent winds, while sea transport eases some of the constraints involved in moving enormous components by road.
Gicon takes another route, raising its hub to 300 m (984 ft) to tap stronger, steadier winds above land. Its 3.8-MW pilot stands taller but has a much lower rated capacity than the Chinese prototype.
It also towers above prominent onshore installations. The Vestas V172-7.2 MW in Winnberg, Germany, reaches 285 m (935 ft) at its highest blade tip, using what Vestas and Max Bögl describe as the world’s tallest series-produced wind-turbine tower. An earlier height-record holder in Gaildorf reaches 246.5 m (809 ft). China’s Sany SI-270150 goes big in a different direction, pairing a 270-m (886-ft) rotor diameter with a 15-MW rated capacity – a different measure of scale from overall height.
To achieve such heights, Gicon’s design combines a conventional wind turbine with a steel lattice support structure and a telescoping inner tower. The mechanism allows the inner tower to rise into its operating position instead of requiring the entire installation to be assembled at its final height. For the final lift, the company used a specialized strand-jacking system, which raises heavy structures using bundles of steel strands. Once extended, the inner tower was secured in its operating position.
Gicon claims its design could produce roughly twice as much electricity as a conventional turbine with the same rotor diameter. The aim is to boost energy yield, not simply chase a bigger power rating. The company envisages future versions with rated capacities exceeding 7 MW, but rated capacity alone does not tell you how much electricity a turbine produces over a month or year. That total is its energy yield.
The company announced completion of the lift on September 29, describing the installation as Germany’s second-tallest structure. According to AP’s report, internal wiring remained to be installed ahead of a planned November 19 inauguration.
Reaching the target height proves a construction milestone, but it does not yet establish annual output, operating costs, or durability. Gicon and SPRIND are preparing a commercialization strategy and are aiming for series production. Preliminary assessments suggest Germany could accommodate up to 4,000 high-altitude towers within existing wind farms. That is an estimate of potential, but it gives the single installation a much bigger job than stealing the height record from China.
Before that ambition becomes a fleet, Schipkau needs to show what the extra altitude buys in practice. Gicon plans to use the findings to develop a wind farm with three to five extra-tall turbines, an intermediate step toward possible full-scale production.

articles.title_orig: A new economic model for the 21st century
articles.title_zh: A new economic model for the 21st century
articles.content_orig:
As the World Bank and IMF reconsider decades of market-led orthodoxy, a deeper debate is emerging over the role of the state, industrial policy and public investment in building resilient, inclusive economies
In the run-up to this year’s International Monetary Fund and World Bank Spring Meetings, the one story that cut through the noise was that the World Bank had embraced industrial policy after decades of advising against it. But while much of the ensuing debate focused on whether this ‘U-turn’ is good or bad, overdue or dangerous, few pondered the fundamental question: What has actually changed?
The World Bank has merely affirmed what many of us have long argued: the framework it has promoted since 1993 – when its East Asian Miracle report cautioned against industrial-policy tools – has not served developing countries well. Such advice, World Bank Chief Economist Indermit Gill recently observed, “has the practical value of a floppy disk today.” Yet in his defence of the report, he also made clear how limited the shift remains. Industrial policy, he argued, should be “targeted and temporary,” an exception to a market-led model, rather than a tool for driving broader economic transformations.
The World Bank’s latest work confirms that industrial policy is more replicable across income levels and institutional contexts than the old consensus admitted, with a toolkit that extends beyond tariffs and subsidies. Public support for private actors, the bank now argues, should come with carrots and sticks, including withdrawal of finance from firms that underperform. This new position aligns with arguments we made in the ‘Entrepreneurial State’ and through more recent work on the role of missions and conditionalities.
But new conclusions do not automatically produce new economics. The World Bank still treats the state as a mere fixer of market failures, rather than as a market creator and shaper. The question is not whether governments should intervene after markets have failed. It is what kind of economy we want to build in the first place. Which public purposes should guide investment, and how can institutions govern the public–private bargain so that value is created collectively and shared fairly?
Viewed in these terms, the bank still falls short, because it treats fiscal-policy space as a fixed constraint within which to optimise, rather than as a set of institutional capacities that can be developed. As a result, the bank would still organise industrial policy only around specific sectors and considerations of comparative advantage. But the energy transition, water and food security, public health, and economic resilience are not sectoral issues. They call for economy-wide missions.
From market fixer to market shaper Nor is the World Bank an isolated case. The IMF’s own economists have similarly documented how austerity and liberalisation fail to deliver. Yet these findings have yet to translate consistently into new operational practices. That needs to change. The IMF and the World Bank sit at the centre of an international order whose default advice still reflects an economics not supported by real-world evidence. What they model, measure and recommend shapes how development and macroeconomic policy are done around the world. They help determine who has access to liquidity, and on what terms; whose debt is treated as sustainable; whose public investment is seen as credible; and whose policy autonomy is constrained. The wealthy countries that fund and control these institutions are not exempt from the consequences of the same economics. For decades, the same flawed assumptions shaped policy in Europe and the US, suppressing public investment, weakening public services, treating wages as costs rather than as fuel for aggregate demand and leaving households exposed to shocks that markets failed to manage. The resulting affordability crisis has now become a political one. The economics that constrained development policy abroad – hollowing out public capacity and narrowing what governments can do – helped fuel the far right at home. Europe’s response to the 2022 energy shock shows what is at stake. From 2022 to 2025, EU member states and the UK incurred $1.8trn in additional costs, much of it absorbed by households and public budgets, while the shareholders of firms charging higher prices benefited. Spain points to an alternative. Having invested in energy security as a mission, rather than as a subsidy category, it now generates more than half of its electricity from renewables, leaving it more insulated than its neighbours from the latest energy shock.
Consistent framework required Making such resilience the default, rather than the exception, requires an economic framework that governments can apply consistently. The Global Progressive Mobilisation, convened by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, recently brought together progressive governments from around the world to start shaping a new economic consensus.
Its foundations are clear. We need public institutions with the capacity to invest, coordinate, and govern markets in the public interest. We need finance designed around missions, not leverage ratios, and policy frameworks that treat fiscal space not as a market-determined ceiling, but as something built by productive investment. And we need measures of value orientated around the common good. The argument for a new economics is being won. Now we must show what comes next.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures edge higher after OpenAI's revenue report prompts tech sector turmoil: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures edge higher after OpenAI's revenue report prompts tech sector turmoil: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stock futures edged higher early Friday after an underwhelming revenue report from OpenAI took some steam out of the high-flying artificial intelligence trade.
S&P 500 futures were up 0.4%, while Nasdaq 100 futures added 0.83%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures advanced 0.15%.
Shares of SpaceX rose 2% in extended trading after the rocket company announced a deal to buy a nationwide spectrum portfolio. Shares of AT&T , Verizon and T-Mobile slid as investors wondered worried the agreement could drive up competition.
AI stocks dropped on Thursday after CNBC confirmed that OpenAI told investors that it saw $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September. Last month, a $68 billion figure was widely reported, though a person familiar with the matter said it also included gross revenue from partners.
CoreWeave fell more than 7%, while Oracle , Intel and Super Micro Computer all lost around 5%. Advanced Micro Device slid close to 4%, while Nvidia shed almost 3%.
"If we have a number of days like this ... we could see a real rout in AI-related names," said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group, on CNBC's "Closing Bell: Overtime." "That could sour investors."
The Nasdaq Composite dropped more than 1%, marking its biggest one-day loss since mid-August. Thursday marked the second down day in a row for the tech-heavy index after it climbed to fresh all-time records earlier in the week.
Tech troubles dragged the S&P 500 to a 0.5% loss, marking its second straight day in the red. But the blue-chip Dow bucked the downtrend, with the 30-stock index ending the session slightly above flat.
The Dow and Nasdaq Composite are both around flat week to date. The broad S&P 500 is on track for a gain of 0.6% for the week.
Investors will monitor Delta Air Lines earnings before the bell on Friday. Consumer sentiment data for October is also expected in the morning.
In Asia on Friday, Japan's Nikkei 225 was little changed, mainland China's CSI 300 advanced 0.16%, while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.64%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.4% in its last hour of trade.
Apple shares were seen around 2% lower in premarket, after Nikkei Asia reported that the company has told some suppliers to cut production of components for its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models. CNBC has reached out to Apple for comment.
Telecoms stocks including AT&T , Verizon and T-Mobile were all sharply lower following a SpaceX deal that will boost its drive to become a mobile carrier competitor in the U.S. SpaceX shares were up nearly 4% early Friday.
Humana meanwhile popped 14% after the insurer was upgraded in closely watched Medicare Advantage quality ratings data.
Treasury yields steadied early Friday as traders assessed President Donald Trump's pledge to not attack Iran until after the midterm elections.
Yields on 10-year U.S. Treasurys — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — were holding firm at 5.2399%.
The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was also unchanged at 5.6139%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was more than 2 basis points higher at 4.7827%.
European stocks popped in early Friday trade, with the regional Stoxx 600 index up 0.8% at 8:18 a.m. in London and many sectors trading more than 1% higher.
Mining stocks led the charge, up 1.8%, amid concerns of a copper supply squeeze due to strikes at several major operations. Retailers were also 1.6% higher.
Telecommunication stocks tumbled more than 2%, with Deutsche Telecom down 7%, after a SpaceX deal that will give the company greater reach in the U.S. telecoms market rattled U.S. incumbent players AT&T , Verizon and T-Mobile in extended trading. Deutsche Telecom is the parent company of T-Mobile US.
Airtel Money, the mobile banking unit of London-listed telecoms group Airtel Africa , is set to begin conditional trading of its shares on Friday ahead of its admission to the London Stock Exchange on Oct. 14.
The company has set 270 million shares at a fixed price of £1.96 ($2.60), implying an estimated market capitalization at admission of £5.3 billion.
Airtel Money reported $1.35 billion in revenue and $676 million in adjusted earnings in the year to June 2026 and has 53 million monthly active users.
The float is expected to be one of the biggest in the U.K. capital since fintech Wise made its £8.75 billion IPO in 2021. Wise has since moved its main listing to New York in a major blow to London, which has lost a steady stream of mid- to large-scale companies in recent years.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said in a September note that investors would be "rejoicing as the UK stock market is finally getting an IPO that isn't a tiny natural resources company," but noted that Airtel Money would not raise new money from the sale, which will come from existing minority shareholders including TPG and the Qatar Investment Authority,
Asia-Pacific markets closed mostly higher Friday.
Mainland China's CSI 300 advanced 0.16% to 4,317.26, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.4% in its last hour of trade.
Japan's Nikkei 225 was little changed at 69,030.92, while the Topix rose 0.33% to 4,104.81.Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.64% to 8,716.6.
South Korean markets were closed for a holiday.
U.S. Treasury yields were largely stable on Friday, with the benchmark 10-year yield falling less than one basis point to 5.227%, while the 30-year yield was little changed at 5.608%.
Both remained near multi-decade highs amid concerns over persistent inflation and elevated government borrowing.
Swiss private bank UBP raised its estimated fair-value range for the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.75%–5.25% in its October outlook, citing renewed inflationary pressures. The bank said in a note on Friday that risks to yields had become more balanced, although visibility remained limited, prompting it to maintain a neutral duration stance of four years and favor income from bond holdings rather than taking directional bets on interest rates.
UBP also expects the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy gradually, with rate cuts unlikely before the second half of 2027.
Oil fell Friday as U.S. President Donald Trump's comments on Iran calmed nerves, following reports that America was considering resuming strikes against Tehran.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery dropped 0.77% to $103.48 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November declined 0.68% to $90.87 per barrel.
Trump said in a post on Truth Social the U.S. "will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," and was having "productive discussions" with Iran.
"In the meantime, accelerated IEA-coordinated stock releases and greater use of alternative export routes could help limit supply pressures," said Thadeu Dos Santos, regional director at markets trading platform Infinox.
"Saudi Arabia's continued use of its restored East-West pipeline is also allowing more crude to reach international markets without relying on the Strait of Hormuz, providing some offset to the upside risks," he added.
Australian AI data center operator Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia , has withdrawn its planned mega initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, the company said in an emailed statement to CNBC.
Firmus said its board determined that the terms of the proposed offering did not adequately reflect the strength of its business and long-term growth outlook.
"The board therefore concluded that proceeding with the offer was not in the best interests of the company and its shareholders," Firmus said in a statement. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options," it added.

articles.title_orig: Experience: I became the world’s oldest crowd surfer at 99
articles.title_zh: Experience: I became the world’s oldest crowd surfer at 99
articles.content_orig:
After retiring at 83, I had a new lease of life creating social media content with my grandson. Then I broke the crowd surfing world record
I n 2013, aged 87, I was playing basketball with my grandson Ross in Ohio while he was home from college. He made a video of me blocking his shot, posted it online, and people really ate it up. We started doing comedy skits together and now have more than 4 million followers on Instagram.
After doing lots of short videos, we decided to make a documentary about my life. As part of it, we compiled my bucket list. One of the things I wanted to do was break a world record. Ross and I spent months thinking of something that would be outrageous, but also fun and inclusive. We settled on me becoming the world’s oldest crowd surfer.
Ross knows the country singer Brantley Gilbert, and he was willing to help us at a show he was playing in Bellville, Texas. Originally, during the crowd surfing, I was going to be strapped to a board Ross had made to protect my back, but it was flexing too much, so he strapped me into a stretcher instead.
I was 99 years and 274 days old the day it happened. It was the first time I’d ever crowd surfed. To break the record, I had to stay up for at least 10 seconds. There were 20,000 people in the crowd – we planned for them to move me in a straight line from the back to the front. But 20 minutes before we were due to start, we saw that everyone in the main crowd was sitting in chairs with gaps between them. Ross started panicking. We used the mosh pit instead, and I travelled in a U-shape from stage right to stage left.
I wore a white T-shirt with a red outline of my face on it so I would stand out from the crowd. Brantley introduced me and said: “I’ll beat you up if you drop Granny.”
I was launched out and I felt as if I was flying. I knew I had to trust everyone. Ross panicked because there was a walkway between both sides of the stage with a 10ft gap and a high fence that I had to be passed over. He jumped the fence as I went across and security people carried me over. I was held up for more than three minutes – nearly an entire song. I was so content. I put my arms out and felt I could touch the sky.
after newsletter promotion
When I got back on the stage, the crowd chanted, “Granny, Granny”. I stood there, soaking it all in. It gave me chills. I was recognised by Guinness World Records for becoming the oldest person to crowd surf at a concert .
Ross comes up with all the ideas. He says he’s Steven Spielberg and I’m Betty White. I only realised how much people liked our videos when I went to the grocery store one day and people were asking to take pictures with me.
This is a whole new life for me. I grew up on a farm in Ohio, the youngest of seven children. We didn’t have TV or a phone. We had chores to do from a young age. During the second world war, I made ammunition in a weapons factory, and I worked in factories until my retirement at 83. I’ve worked hard – it gave me purpose.
The videos are a new kind of work. Meeting people is my favourite part. I’ve met Pope Leo and celebrities like Tom Holland and Bad Bunny on red carpets. I love meeting people who know us from social media. They come up to me and say: “I was lonely and sad in hospital and I watched your videos to lift me up.” People say they’ve reconnected with family after watching Ross and I together. When I’m on my deathbed, I want to know that we made everybody’s day a little better.
I took care of Ross when he was a baby, but this has brought us closer. Before, I only saw him a handful of times a year, but now we live together in Ohio.
I turned 100 this summer, and I had two parties with hundreds of people. I can’t believe I’m 100. I’m the only one out of my siblings who has lived this long. Not all days are peachy. The hardest part of getting older is the aches and pains. Making our videos gives me a purpose, and that boosts me on days I don’t feel so good.
I hope our videos make people realise that it’s never too late to live your best life. If you want to do something new, do it now. Enjoy every moment, because it goes by in the blink of an eye.

articles.title_orig: Finland: The world's happiest nation faces a glum winter
articles.title_zh: Finland: The world's happiest nation faces a glum winter
articles.content_orig:
There's an uneasy mood in Finland — the country ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years . A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years.
With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.
Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.
Last month, Statistics Finland confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was about 65%.
Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.
Yet, the Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 Global Financial Crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.
Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.
"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's Monetary Policy and Research Department, told DW.
Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to at least 2% of GDP by 2031.

Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to date to promise a further €9 billion in cuts, if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.
While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes, meaning public services will bear the brunt.
Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."
While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.
With household spending already falling, Lauri Olappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.
"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Olappa told DW.
Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the impact of two wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.
Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.
During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
In April, the government said it would further hike defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.

With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war , the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.
While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear reactor in 2023, has cushioned a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.
On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Olappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.
"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.
Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.
On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.
That is, as long as the next shock is not a longer oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a euro-area debt crisis centered on France.
Next March, Finland could yet be named the planet’s happiest nation for a 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.
Edited by: Kristie Pladson

articles.title_orig: Beyond the Medal: Judo’s Principles at the Heart of Competition
articles.title_zh: Beyond the Medal: Judo’s Principles at the Heart of Competition
articles.content_orig:
Yet even at this highest level, where every detail can decide a contest, judo remains rooted in the principles established by Jigoro Kano.
Competition is part of judo. It is an important part, certainly, but it is one element of a much broader path. On the tatami in Baku, athletes seek victory with total commitment, but they do so within a framework built on respect, discipline and mutual recognition. Before and after every contest, there is the bow. It may last only a moment but it carries the essence of the sport: respect for the opponent, for the referee, for the rules and for the place in which judo is practised.
The rules themselves are not simply a structure for deciding who wins and who loses. They protect the athletes and preserve the technical identity of judo. They make it possible for determination, intelligence, courage and skill to be expressed fairly. At this level, athletes know that they are accountable not only for the result but also for the way they pursue it.
Every champion seen on the tatami this week began as a child in a dojo. Before the medals, the television cameras and the national expectations, there were first falls, first bows, first lessons on how to hold a partner, how to listen and how to stand back up. There were years of learning, progression and doubt. Becoming a competitor is one stage in that journey, a demanding and valuable one, but it is not the final destination.
For some, competition will lead to world titles and Olympic medals. For others, it will lead to coaching, refereeing, education, administration or a lifelong connection with their club and community. The lessons remain the same. Judo teaches people how to face success with humility and defeat with dignity. It teaches responsibility towards others, because progress is never achieved alone. Every judoka develops through training partners, coaches, families, officials and opponents.
This is where the principles of Seiryoku Zenyo, the best use of energy, and Jita Kyoei, mutual welfare and benefit, find their full meaning. They are not abstract ideas reserved for the dojo wall. They are present in every bow, every act of fair play and every moment when a competitor recognises the value of the person standing opposite them.
A world championship is a celebration of elite sport. It is also a reminder that judo is bigger than a medal table. The champions of today are the children of yesterday, and they will become the mentors, leaders and examples of tomorrow. In that continuity lies one of judo’s greatest strengths.

By Phillip Broadwith 2026-10-09T08:05:00+01:00
The 2026 Nobel prize in chemistry has been awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai , ‘for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis’. The prize recognises the pair’s contribution to understanding the very fundamentals of how we can influence and control the handedness of chiral molecules.
Asymmetric synthesis is a cornerstone of modern drug development, as well as being important for flavours, fragrances and agrochemicals. But chiral molecules also crop up in liquid crystals, polymers and optical materials, as well as across various classes of speciality chemicals. Almost all these products rely, at some point, on catalysts that can transform achiral or racemic molecules into products in which one enantiomer is massively – if not exclusively – dominant.
Source: © Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images
This year’s prize recognises truly fundamental science that has had huge bearing on the commercial applications of asymmetric catalysis
When you’re aiming to make chiral molecules for commercial sale, an efficient synthesis has a significant effect on cost – and hence profitability. Cleaner reactions mean less wasted materials, as well as less time and resources spent on separation and purification. Understanding how to create more effective catalysts, which can drive higher yields and selectivity, can translate into a huge competitive advantage.
Henri Kagan and his team’s insight into the intricacies of how catalysts can be manipulated to drastically improve their performance underlies all this development. Likewise, there are different approaches to enantio-enrichment, as Kenso Soai and his team’s autocatalytic experiments showed.
This year’s laureates didn’t invent asymmetric synthesis, but filled in some key aspects in our understanding of how it works and how we can do it better. This fundamental research has naturally stimulated many other researchers to ask further questions, digging deeper into how these reactions work and further advancing our understanding of chirality and catalysis.
That, in turn, shows up in the applications: new and better catalyst systems have allowed us to build ever more complex molecules in more efficient ways, and directly enabled the wide commercial availability of chiral reagents and chemical building blocks. A fact that’s worth remembering next time you’re browsing through a catalogue, planning your next synthesis.

Shares were mostly higher Friday in Europe and Asia, while oil prices fell back from recent gains.
U.S. futures edged higher.
In early European trading, the German DAX rose 0.7% to 24,975.62, while the CAC 40 in Paris surged 0.8% to 7,789.91. Britain's FTSE 100 picked up 0.7% to 10,515.43.
The future for the S&P 500 was up 0.4%, while that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.1%.
In Asian trading, Tokyo's Nikkei 225 closed nearly unchanged at 69,030.92.
The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.1% higher, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng rallied 1.6% to 24,152.44.
China is due to release its latest economic growth figures next week.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.6% to 8,716.60, while the Sensex in India added 1.2%.
Markets were closed in South Korea and Taiwan.
U.S. stocks were unsteady Thursday, as oil prices rose and bond yields jumped before receding later in the day.
“Equities remain within striking distance of record highs, but the backdrop has turned considerably less hospitable,” Steven Innes of SPI Asset Management said in a commentary.
The S&P 500 fell 0.5% for a second straight loss after setting an all-time high the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.1%, and the Nasdaq composite fell 1.3% as technology stocks took particularly hard hits.
Stocks felt pressure from a 4.1% rise in the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, to $104.28. It’s been pinballing between $96 and nearly $110 over the last month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.
Brent got to nearly $106 in the morning before President Donald Trump sent its price veering after saying “productive discussions” are happening with Iran and that the U.S. military would not attack it before the upcoming U.S. elections in November.
Early Friday, Brent was down 1% at $103.28 a barrel, while U.S. benchmark crude oil was 0.8% lower, at $90.75 a barrel.
In the bond market , yields have been trading at their highest levels in years or even decades, threatening to slow the economy.
The 10-year Treasury yield initially rose to 5.35% early Thursday before falling back to 5.23%.
It dropped after the U.S. government said that it sold $22 billion in 30-year Treasury bonds at an auction with a high yield of less than 5.62%. That helped bring the 30-year Treasury yield down to 5.60% from 5.73% in the morning, which is a notable move for the bond market.
High debt loads have loomed over the market as the U.S. federal deficit climbed to nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended on Sept. 30.
In share trading, PepsiCo climbed 3.7% after it reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. But drops for several influential technology stocks overshadowed those gains.
Nvidia, the chip company that’s ridden the tidal wave of demand created by artificial-intelligence technology, fell 2.9%. Because it’s the largest stock by value on Wall Street, it was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 even though other stocks had larger losses.
That included drops for other AI-related stocks. Broadcom lost 4.3% and Micron Technology slumped 4.8%.
AI stocks are under heavy pressure to report big growth to justify how expensive their shares have gotten due to the AI frenzy.
“What was once a broad, buy-anything-with-an-AI-label momentum trade is becoming a much tougher contest between balance-sheet strength and ambition,” Innes said.
In other dealings early Friday, the U.S. dollar rose to 158.37 Japanese yen from 157.89 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1228, up from $1.1211.

articles.title_orig: Made in Nebraska: Combines built for the world
articles.title_zh: Made in Nebraska: Combines built for the world
articles.content_orig:
CNH builds the Case IH Axial-Flow series and 260 series combines at its manufacturing plant along Highway 281 in Grand Island, Neb.
Andy Dozler grew up on a farm near Albion, Neb., operating red Case IH equipment in his family’s fields. And yes, he does bleed Case IH red.
Today, when Dozler is driving down the road and sees a Case IH AF series combine — voted in 2025 as the “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” — working in the field, he can say with great pride that his team and at the Case IH manufacturing plant in Grand Island, Neb., built that combine.
In fact, at that plant, they build Case IH AF series and 260 series combines that are sold around the globe, with each combine individually customized for a specific location and buyer.
For Dozler, this is his dream job. After graduating from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, he took a job with CNH, the parent company of Case IH, as a quality engineer. He spent a little over a year at the New Holland, Pa., plant, where he worked on the round baler, square baler and pull-type silage chopper.
He started at the Grand Island plant in 2006, working his way up through the engineering department. Today, Dozler is the manufacturing engineering manager at the plant, leading a team of 20 engineers and six tool-and-die operators. And he gets to be on the ground level of researching, developing and building Case IH combines and other farm equipment for the world.
Andy Dozler, an Albion, Neb., native and University of Nebraska-Lincoln graduate, serves as the manufacturing engineering manager at the Case IH plant in Grand Island. He was involved in the development of the new Case IH AF series combines that won the 2025 “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” award last fall.
During a recent plant tour, Dozler told Nebraska Farmer that his engineering team was intimately involved in the development of the revolutionary AF series combines. Exploration for the development of a Class 10+ combine started as far back as 2011 for Case IH.
The first prototype was built in 2013, and by 2023, a combine was built in a special bay at the Grand Island plant. The first commercial AF combine rolled off the assembly line in March 2024.
For the AF9, AF10 and AF11, the grain tank capacity ranges from 455 bushels up to 567 bushels, and the unload rate goes from 4.5 bushels per second up to 6 bushels per second. With a feeder width of 56 inches, and peak horsepower ranging in the series from 635 hp up to 775 hp, these combines have more capacity than any other Case IH combine made to date.
It was all part of the plan as the new models were developed, Dozler said, as he described the responsibilities of his engineering team at the plant.
“Our team consists of advanced manufacturing engineers who support future programs, as well as assembly, weld, test, fabrication and tool design engineers,” he said. “Our tool-and-die operators are responsible for building new tools and fixtures, as well as repairing and reworking existing fixtures.”
On the manufacturing engineering side, their highest responsibility is to keep the production lines running. “We accomplish this by quickly addressing fit-up issues, quality concerns and missing-part situations,” Dozler said.
They also review design changes, determining how those changes will affect the plant, and develop the bills of materials required to build the products and determine the tooling and equipment needed — including torque tools, weld fixtures and assembly equipment. They figure out crucial timing and sequence for implementing engineering changes on the production lines.
With each combine produced at the plant, whether that is a 260 or AF series, the engineers determine where parts and processes should be incorporated into the production lines and ensure the lines remain properly balanced.
“Our team continuously works on quality improvement, safety and cost-reduction projects,” Dozler added. “Overall, our manufacturing engineering plays a key role in supporting current production while preparing the plant for future products and process changes.”
Combines aren’t the only pieces of new farm machinery rolling out of Grand Island. The plant builds Case IH windrowers, disk headers and sicklebar headers, along with New Holland bale wagons and self-propelled windrowers.
Farmers who purchase new Case IH combines can tour the plant in Grand Island, Neb., watch their own combine as it is built, start their combine for the first time and even drive it off the production line.
The plant was opened as Sperry New Holland in 1965. After years of expansion and corporate acquisitions, the 165-acre site in Grand Island — which includes a main campus of three manufacturing buildings and a warehouse north of the plant — has produced a myriad of forage and harvest equipment. It continues to employ hundreds of workers, shipping farm equipment to 34 countries.
Dozler said that plenty of farmers tour the plant and watch their own new combine as it is built at the factory. This experience includes the culmination of being able to start the machine for the first time and even drive it off the production line.
Watching satisfied customers is one of the great joys Dozler receives from his job, along with the thrill of watching those combines made in Grand Island in the field bringing in another harvest.
The competition for “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” is sponsored by the Nebraska Manufacturing Alliance, with support from Pinnacle Bank. In this March Madness-style tournament, voters decide which nominated inventions and products advance to the finals.
Every year, agriculture takes a center stage spot in the voting, with Valley center pivots taking the prize in 2024 and the Case IH AF series combine winning in 2025. Voting for the 2026 winners closed Oct. 4.
Learn more at nemanufacturingalliance.com .

Curt Arens began writing about Nebraska’s farm families when he was in high school. Before joining Farm Progress first as a field editor in 2010, and then as editor of Nebraska Farmer in 2021, he had worked as a freelance farm writer for 27 years for newspapers and farm magazines, including Nebraska Farmer. His real full-time career during this period was farming his family’s fourth-generation land near Crofton, Neb., where his family raised corn, soybeans, wheat, oats, alfalfa, cattle, hogs and Christmas trees.
Curt and his wife, Donna, have four children: Lauren, Taylor, Zachary and Benjamin. They are active in their church and St. Rose School in Crofton, where Donna teaches. The family now rents out their crop ground to a neighbor, but still lives on the same farm first operated by Curt's great-grandparents. The family runs a few cows and other assorted 4-H and FFA critters.
Previously, the 1986 University of Nebraska animal science graduate wrote a weekly rural life column, developed a farm radio program and wrote books about farm life. Isaias’ sustained winds remain at 105 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center’s 2 a.m. ET update. NOAA and Air Force hurricane hunters are flying inside the storm, now about 230 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
Isaias could briefly become a Category 3 hurricane Friday before weakening somewhat and making landfall late at night. Even as Isaias is expected to lose some strength before landfall, it will still bring dangerous storm surge, damaging winds and flooding rain.
Residents across coastal Alabama and Florida spent Thursday boarding up homes, filling sandbags and stocking up on supplies as Hurricane Isaias strengthened into a Category 2 storm and barreled toward the Gulf Coast.
AP video from Lillian, Alabama, showed residents covering windows with plywood and loading supplies as they prepare to ride out the storm. “Everybody’s getting fuel. Everybody’s buying water. Everybody’s scurrying around like ants,” resident Richard Weekley said.
Reuters video from Gulf Breeze, Florida, showed residents filling and loading sandbags as they prepare for possible flooding from Hurricane Isaias.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned that saturated ground and heavy rainfall could cause dangerous inland flooding, urging residents to take the threat seriously.
Forecasters said Isaias is expected to make landfall late Friday, with life-threatening storm surge, flooding rain and possible tornadoes forecast across parts of Florida, Alabama and Mississippi.
An eye is beginning to take shape as lightning flashes within Isaias’ thunderstorms over the Gulf.
The emerging eye points to a better-organized hurricane, while the lightning near the center of the storm signals vigorous thunderstorm activity in the eyewall as Isaias strengthens tonight.
A remarkable sunset unfolded over Atlanta on Thursday. CNN meteorologist Derek Van Dam explains how distant Hurricane Isaias in the Gulf created the spectacle.
Isaias’ sustained winds have increased to 105 mph, and the National Hurricane Center now forecasts it will briefly become a major hurricane early Friday. “Major” refers to a Category 3 or stronger storm, with sustained winds of at least 111 mph.
Isaias should weaken some before landfall, likely coming ashore near the threshold between Category 1 and 2 late Friday night. However, its wind field is expected to expand, spreading dangerous impacts well beyond its center.
Isaias is in infamous company as an “I” named storm.
The list of names runs alphabetically, so “I” goes to the ninth named storm — which usually forms around the peak of Atlantic hurricane season in mid-September, when conditions are primed to fuel powerful storms. And since 1953, Atlantic storms with “I” names reach Category 3 strength or higher more frequently than any other letter.
Ivan in 2004, Irma in 2017, Ida in 2021 and most recently Ian in 2022 each reached at least Category 4 strength and went on to make landfall in the United States. Ian struck southwestern Florida with 150 mph winds, resulted in 150 deaths and caused over $112 billion in damage, becoming the costliest hurricane in the state’s history.
Storms that are especially deadly or damaging have their name retired from the official list. Thirteen names starting with I have been retired, more than any other letter.
Isaias formed on October 6, weeks later than usual for an “I” storm, thanks to this year’s super El Niño putting a damper on storms in the Atlantic. It’s currently forecast to make landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 1 or Category 2 hurricane.
Isaias is expected to strengthen overnight as it passes near a warm eddy, a rotating pocket of ocean water where warmth extends well below the surface. That deep reservoir of heat, marked by the darker reds in the image below, provides ample fuel for the hurricane.
Increasing wind shear is expected to weaken Isaias as it approaches the coast, but it is still forecast to make landfall as a dangerous hurricane.
Winds in Hurricane Isaias reached around 100 mph today, according to Captain Mark McCoy, an Air Force Reserve Weather officer who flew through the storm.
He told CNN’s Erin Burnett that his team experienced “a lot of dry air” that “was being sucked in on the south side and southwest side.”
“It was slowly gaining strength as we were in there,” McCoy said.
The journey, which he said was a “pretty standard mission,” lasted around 9.5 hours and included flying through the eye of the storm.
Isaias is still a Category 2 hurricane with 100 mph sustained winds as of the 7 p.m. CT update from the National Hurricane Center.
After intensifying earlier today, the storm’s strength has leveled off … for now. Further strengthening is expected through early Friday.
Hurricane Isaias is beginning to pick up speed, traveling at a 13 mph pace which is up from 9 mph reported about 12 hours ago. The hurricane is located just under 300 miles south of Louisiana.
It’s forecast to turn north tomorrow and approach the Gulf Coast later that night.
Before Hurricane Isaias makes landfall along the Gulf Coast, officials as far as Charleston, South Carolina, are already preparing for lingering effects from the hurricane.
On Thursday, Charleston Mayor William S. Cogswell Jr. activated the city’s active flood mitigation plan, anticipating heavy rain and as a king tide cycle brings risk of flooding over the weekend to the coastal city on the Atlantic.
The most intense rain affecting Charleston is expected on Saturday afternoon into the evening, with city officials expecting 3 to 4 inches of rain, though it could be higher in some areas, a city news release said. Tides in Charleston’s harbor are expected to peak near 7.7 feet Saturday morning and remain high into the evening.

articles.title_orig: World Bank and IMF’s lack of climate action could make countries bystanders in their own destruction
articles.title_zh: World Bank and IMF’s lack of climate action could make countries bystanders in their own destruction
articles.content_orig:
© World Economic Forum / Benedikt von Loebell
The World Bank and IMF are shifting away from explicit climate action towards resilience, reflecting political pressure from the US that weakens their response to global heating, argues Federico Sibaja  and Jon Sward.
The authors criticise the World Bank’s approach after its financing supported a Nepal hydropower project that was damaged by devastating floods despite warnings and the absence of a proper climate-risk assessment.
Meanwhile, IMF-backed austerity and fossil-fuel policies in countries including Ecuador and Pakistan are limiting investment in climate adaptation and, in some cases, undermining the shift to renewable energy.
With climate-vulnerable countries facing mounting damage, the authors argue that institutions must expand grant-based finance and debt relief, and ensure climate risks are built into lending decisions and economic programmes.
In a recent interview with the New York Times , World Bank President Ajay Banga explained that the bank wants to avoid the “emotional” debate around climate change and instead focus on resilient investments.
For the leader of an institution that describes itself as the “knowledge bank”, such a desire to skirt the realities of climate science is of course the result of political calculus.
The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, has also shifted gears in recent years: she went from calling for an end to “business as usual” at COP28 , to agreeing with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the need to refocus away from climate change. She has also cut the budget earmarked for climate work by 27%.
Meanwhile, Bessent has questioned the cause of global warming and referred to climate action at global financial institutions as driven by “elite beliefs” .
The World Bank and IMF’s change in approach comes as no surprise, as there is a potentially steep cost of them falling afoul of their largest shareholder, amid its wider war on multilateralism.
But what’s been less discussed is the wider cost of the Bretton Woods institutions’ failure to act in the midst of an accelerating climate emergency – of which the serious flooding in Bangkok, where the World Bank and IMF convene their annual meetings next week, is a stark reminder.
After a prolonged debate on the future of the bank’s climate commitments in the Spring, a compromise was reached in June , when it extended its climate change action plan (CCAP) “indefinitely”, but retired its 45% climate finance target.
As the US’s anti-climate action agenda has cast a long shadow at the institution and elsewhere since last year, bank officials increasingly say their goal is to deliver resilient investments, echoing Banga’s recent statements.
However, there are serious questions about whether the bank’s approach is advancing its aim.
The recent flood disaster in Nepal, which killed more than 1,450 people (with around 5,800 still missing), also damaged 13 hydropower projects, including the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower plant. Alongside other lenders , Trishuli was backed by financing from the World Bank’s private investment arm , IFC, and a US$87.4mn guarantee from its political risk arm, MIGA. Yet, despite repeated warnings from an independent expert panel, no climate and disaster risk assessment had been properly undertaken as of 2024.
The World Bank needs to ensure that “resilience” is more than an empty signifier. This means having mechanisms in place across all lending instruments to evaluate whether its actions are genuinely leading to positive outcomes for people and the planet, including ex-post assessments of projects that emphasise learning from past mistakes.
It also means rethinking the the bank’s neoliberal era loan conditions in its policy based lending , which have promoted wholesale privatisation in key sectors like energy, and ensuring countries have the policy and fiscal space to pursue green industrial policy .
As evidenced by the Nepal crisis, with the country facing an estimated US$4.7bn in reconstruction costs, climate-vulnerable countries also urgently need a rapid scaling up of grant-based climate finance and debt relief . The World Bank could use its convening role to help move this discussion forward.
The IMF’s relevance has grown due to increasingly frequent shocks to the global economy, such as spikes in fossil fuel prices and extreme weather events. In July 2026 , 30 countries were implementing IMF programmes with conditionalities, and 14 other countries were seeking new arrangements.
Recent analysis has shown that its programmes’ reliance on fiscal consolidation and foreign exchange accumulation can undermine countries’ climate policy goals and put macroeconomic stability – Bessent’s  “focus” of the IMF – at risk. So, while the IMF has become better at diagnosing climate risk, it is also exacerbating it.
For example, in Ecuador, the IMF-backed programme requires primary adjustment of 6.6% of GDP. Such fiscal adjustment can make it harder to invest in climate adaptation and resilient infrastructure. At the same time, the programme explicitly aims to increase oil output.
The same goes for Pakistan. The country has been on the frontlines of the climate crisis in the last few years, with devastating floods in 2022. Yet IMF-backed fiscal consolidation has constrained spending at a time when the country faces enormous adaptation needs. Moreover, reforms in fiscal policy are undermining the energy transition: due to IMF-led energy subsidy removal and tariff increases, the country began a rapid shift to solar, only to see it undermined by IMF-backed higher taxes on solar panels.
Back in June, the IMF’s own independent evaluation office flagged this contradiction. It identified the review of progam design and conditionality , the process through which the institution evaluates the performance of its lending programmes and agrees ways to improve them, as a chance to address it. Yet, when the review wrapped up last month, climate was firmly excluded .
As more countries turn to the IMF to address their vulnerability to shocks, its push for fiscal adjustment and commodity extraction risks accelerating that same vulnerability.
At the upcoming annual meetings, we need to see serious efforts to resolve this contradiction. A good place to start would be the guidance the IMF provides to staff designing loan programmes, which will be developed in the next few months. This must clearly outline under what circumstances climate goals are central to programme success and cannot be ignored.
Without a change of course, the IMF and World Bank will miss a key window of opportunity to stem a runaway climate crisis. In the present context, delaying action is just another form of climate denial.

An economist from the Universidad de Buenos Aires, he is an expert on the interactions between debt and climate policy. He has extensive experience in policymaking, research and campaigning across Argentina, Belgium and internationally.
Jon Sward is environment project manager at the Bretton Woods Project, where he oversees its climate advocacy work towards the World Bank and the IMF. He holds a PhD from the School of Global Studies at the University of Sussex.

Police say man taken to hospital and mayor says child physically unharmed as he condemns ‘unconscionable’ act
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and injured a man in New York City on Thursday afternoon during an enforcement operation, federal officials said.
The man was conscious and hospitalized, authorities said , and the shooting quickly sparked angry protests from local residents and elected officials in the neighborhood.
Early reports indicated that agents had surrounded the man and a five-year-old child in his car in a residential area before firing multiple rounds, the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, said in a statement on Thursday evening. The child was physically unharmed, he said.
“I have been on ​the phone with President Trump and [Homeland Security] secretary Mullin negotiating ‌the release of the man ICE agents ‌shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful,” Mamdani told a press conference. He demanded from the Trump ‌administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City, he said.
The shooting took place at roughly 4pm in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx, according to the New York police department (NYPD).
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement on social media that ICE officers were conducting an operation targeting an undocumented man from the Dominican Republic. The statement did not explain what led to the shooting, saying: “During the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured.”
The extent of the man’s injuries was unknown. The department’s statement alleged that the man had “associations” with a gang and prior criminal convictions, but DHS did not name the man or provide evidence of his background. The department has previously faced backlash for falsely accusing immigrants of being gang members after they were shot by agents .
DHS spokespeople did not immediately respond to questions about what led to the shooting, the extent of the man’s injuries, or the reports that a five-year-old was in the car during the shooting.
New York’s police commissioner, Jessica Tisch, said the NYPD had located the child with a family member after a wellness check. She alleged the man ​– identified as a 28-year-old – had been arrested twice in New York City in 2023 and 2025.
Cellphone vide o published by the New York Times appeared to show the immediate aftermath of the shooting, with an agent in a yellow vest holding what appeared to be an assault rifle while talking on the phone. The newspaper s aid other witness video appeared to show several agents in the middle of the street in the aftermath, with one armed and another restraining a man on the ground.
One witness told the City Reporter, a local news outlet, that she saw a man bleeding on the ground in front of a car and observed an agent holding a small child. Videos also showed bullet holes in the windshield of an SUV, NY1 reported.
Mamdani expressed outrage in an earlier post on X, saying: “I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities. Our thoughts are with the injured New Yorker and his family tonight. We are praying for his recovery. Get ICE out of our neighborhoods. Get ICE out of our hospitals. Get ICE off our streets. Get ICE away from our children.”
The mayor ended his statement with: “Abolish ICE.”
Protesters began to gather in the area soon after the shooting, with some demonstrators holding signs saying, “Jail all killer ICE agents” and “Leave our neighbors alone”.
Hands Off NYC and the New York Immigration Coalition, two local groups, held an emergency press conference in the area where elected officials and organizers expressed outrage and decried ICE’s ongoing presence in the neighborhood.
“ICE, get the fuck out of our neighborhood,” shouted Vanessa Gibson, Bronx borough president. “I’m angry that we have to be here … We are a working-class community. We don’t deserve this type of treatment from the White House.” She encouraged the crowd to get involved in opposing ICE, saying: “There are more of us than there are of them. I want this to be a moment that we turn into a movement.”
Jumaane Williams, the city’s elected public advocate, said “fuck ICE” and “fuck Trump”, adding: “It is our time to stand up. Those of us who have more privilege – we must take more risk to protect those who don’t.”
New Yorkers of all ages flowed into the streets from the nearby 1 train, and protesters soon also gathered at a local hospital where the man shot by ICE was reported to be receiving treatment. Outside the hospital, NYPD set up barricades and protesters quickly clashed with police officers in a chaotic scene.
Demonstrators banged drums and shouted, “Shut it down,” and “ICE out!” as cars driving by honked in support.
Standing outside the hospital, Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, told the Guardian he wanted to see an independent investigation into the shooting led by New York officials. He also called on DHS to release footage of the shooting and for the officer who fired the shots to face prosecution.
“The pain that you’re witnessing is people who are witnessing their neighbors, their family members, their friends being ripped away,” he said.
DHS has faced growing backlash over immigration officers’ use of deadly force in the field over the last year. Last month, an immigration officer shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, while he was in his car during a traffic stop in Texas. Federal prosecutors then charged the man with assault , alleging he had struck an officer with his side mirror while trying to drive away.
The Trump administration has repeatedly accused immigrants and protesters of “weaponizing” their vehicles, alleging that agents fired their weapons in response to “vehicular attacks”, but a Guardian analysis in July found most of those claims touted by federal officials have fallen apart under scrutiny .
Since Trump returned to office last year, US immigration officers have shot at least two dozen people, according to one analysis , including three US citizens who were killed .
The shooting comes as ICE arrests have hit record levels , with the agency pivoting from the high-profile raids it carried out last year and instead more quietly dispatching agents into communities across the country.

articles.title_orig: What smart people are saying about the US suspending PERM visas for Microsoft, Adobe, and Indian tech giants
articles.title_zh: What smart people are saying about the US suspending PERM visas for Microsoft, Adobe, and Indian tech giants
articles.content_orig:
For foreign workers at some of the biggest employers in tech, there's another twist in an already uncertain system.
The Trump administration’s decision to suspend Microsoft, Adobe, and other named tech companies from the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program has renewed debate over whether stricter skilled-immigration policies protect American workers or hurt American businesses.
On Thursday morning, Vice President JD Vance announced the suspension at a press conference. He singled out Microsoft , saying: "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants."
PERM is not itself a visa. It is the Labor Department certification employers generally need before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based green card. Vance said that some companies had abused the system and used foreign workers to undercut Americans.
In a statement on Thursday, Microsoft disputed Vance's accusations, saying most of its H-1B filings were for existing employees rather than new hires.
"Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people," the company wrote.
Besides Microsoft and Adobe, the action also affected six major IT services companies with deep ties to India’s tech sector: Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, and Capgemini.
Here’s what immigration-policy experts and Indian tech voices are saying:
Hira, a Howard University political science professor and a longtime critic of the H-1B program, called the move against Microsoft “very significant.”
Hira has long argued that employers can use the program in ways that depress pay and disadvantage US workers. He told the Associated Press on Thursday that there are supposed to be protections requiring employers to show that hiring an H-1B worker does not hurt similarly employed Americans.
“That’s never been enforced,” Hira said.
Rand, a former senior advisor at US Citizenship and Immigration Services during the Biden administration, took the opposite view. He called Vance’s announcement “incoherent” in a statement to AP.
Rand’s argument is that the policy could worsen the problem Vance says he wants to solve. H-1B workers are generally tied to their employers for their immigration status. A green card gives workers far more freedom to switch jobs and bargain over pay.
“If the Trump administration were truly concerned that H-1B workers are ‘indentured servants,’ then the last thing they would do is block companies from helping their own H-1B workers get green cards,” Rand told AP.
Pai, an India-based vice president of investments at the country's largest brokerage Zerodha, reacted to what a more restrictive US path to permanent residency could mean for India.
In a statement on X, Pai wrote that the immediate downside could be fewer high-earning Indians in the US, which in turn could mean lower remittances, less soft power, and less angel investments flowing back into Indian startups. He also noted that India receives roughly $125 billion in annual remittances, with the US accounting for about a quarter of that total.
But he also saw a potential upside. If US companies cannot bring talent to America, he wrote, “they probably will bring the work to India.”
US visa uncertainty may also keep more top engineers in India to build domestic companies and AI startups, he added.
Nasscom, India's main tech industry group, said immigration policy and skilled-talent mobility should be treated as separate issues.
"While the decision affects a specific immigration pathway, Nasscom has consistently maintained that immigration and skilled talent mobility are two distinct issues and should not be viewed through the same lens," the group said in a statement to local media
It also said the number of employees moving from H-1B status to permanent residency through PERM is “relatively limited.”

By MARTIN ROBINSON, CHIEF REPORTER
Published: 10:43 EDT, 8 October 2026 | Updated: 20:50 EDT, 8 October 2026
Prince Harry has revealed he felt depressed and 'useless' immediately after Megxit, and now refuses to spend more than ten days away from Meghan and their children.
In a new video released today, the Duke of Sussex claims life in the Royal Family left him unable to properly grieve the death of Princess Diana , adding that his official duties triggered panic attacks.
Harry, 42, said getting dressed for royal engagements in a shirt and tie frequently left him feeling as though he was being strangled or suffocated.
'You would think I had the best help in the world. I'm a prince, for God's sake, but I was still grieving and didn't have any place to put those feelings,' he said, describing emotions he carried for '15 or 20 years'.
He revealed therapy eventually helped him and described the extraordinary moment when spraying himself with Diana's perfume prompted his hidden memories and emotions to come flooding back.
Speaking about grief in a video for the American education platform MasterClass, Harry said despite finding happiness with Meghan, he 'slipped into depression ' after they quit royal life and left Britain.
'We moved to Canada to get some space away from everything and simply think,' he said. 'Within two or three days of leaving that stressful environment, I experienced an adrenaline crash unlike anything I'd ever felt before.
'It was as though I needed stress for my brain to function. I became useless around the house. I slipped into depression for about two weeks and felt like I couldn't function without adrenaline.'
His frank comments about mental health and PTSD came as Meghan Markle stepped back into the spotlight yesterday for the first time in years, wearing a £28,000 outfit to take afternoon tea with Malala Yousafzai in London.

Meghan Markle made her first public appearance in the UK for four years, meeting Malala Yousafzai for afternoon tea at Claridge's yesterday
Meghan and Malala enjoyed smiled as they said farewell following their tea yesterday
Six years on from Megxit, the Sussexes are parents to two children, Archie and Lilibet, and are back in the UK again. The children have started school in the Cotswolds.
And Harry now says that he follows a strict 'ten-day' rule to protect his happiness.
He said: 'The biggest factor for me is the energy, joy and happiness I get from being with my family, especially our children, and from being on the ground doing my work.
'The key to maintaining that balance is spending no more than ten days away from my wife and kids.
'It's about balancing my work and sense of purpose with being a dad and a husband.'
Harry revealed he did not cry for almost 20 years after his mother's death and thinks of her 'pretty much every night and then most mornings'.
A therapist encouraged him to find Diana's perfume in an effort to unlock his grief after he had forgotten what her voice and laugh sounded like.
The Duke said doing this had a remarkable effect on him and his grief, claiming the scent brought back memories and emotions that had long been suppressed.
'It was like being transported to another time,' Harry said. 'It unlocked everything that had been locked away.
'Spraying my mother's scent was almost like knocking certain bricks through so that I could see through and certain memories and experiences could start seeping back.'
In the very personal MasterClass episode – entitled Redefining Grief: Building Resilience Through Loss – Harry also said: 'Everything I do, everything I put my energy towards, I hope that my mother will be proud of.
'Trying to continue and protect her legacy, what I didn't realise was that the work I was drawn to was so similar to the work she was doing.'
Speaking to neuroscientist Dr Mary-Frances O'Connor ahead of World Mental Health Day on Saturday, Harry added that after marrying Meghan and becoming a father, he often felt guilty about allowing himself to be happy.
The interview comes weeks after the publication of his uncle's memoir about Diana, which reignited debate about her legacy and included claims that angered the King.
Earl Spencer claimed in one angry phone call Charles told him Diana would soon be forgotten after she died in Paris in 1997.
Reflecting on his mother's death, Harry said: 'I didn't cry when I was told my mum died, only at her burial, and then not again for nearly two decades.
'I was convinced that was strength, but it wasn't. It was a 12-year-old boy with no permission to fall apart and no roadmap for how to heal.
'I'd spent so long emotionally numb because I felt disloyal and guilty at the possibility of being happy without her. I felt I had to stay sad and emotionally shut down to prove I missed her.'
Harry has explained how therapy transformed his outlook, saying: 'The reality is that what I discovered was that she just wanted me to be happy.
'That was a huge mental shift for me. It freed me and gave me a completely different outlook on life.'
Harry also said that joining the Army gave him a sense of purpose.
'For 15 or 20 years, when people asked, "Are you okay?" my answer was always, "I'm fine". It was numbness. It was emotional shutdown.
'Without realising it, adrenaline was driving me. It was the force that led me to join the military at 20. It was the perfect distraction.'
The Duke said he increasingly withdrew from his friends and social life during those years, explaining how he 'was much more comfortable sitting at home'.

Harry added that he struggled to find help at first.
'Unfortunately, a number of general practitioners weren't equipped to help me. It was a case of receiving advice or being offered a pill.
'I was completely against taking medication. I followed the advice but it wasn't making any difference, so I kept searching for something that would work.'
He described his deployment to Afghanistan as life-changing.
'The things I saw and experienced appeared to trigger other traumas that had been stored within me,' he said.
Harry said therapy eventually gave him the 'permission to grieve'.
'Sitting in a room with a complete stranger and having the confidence and trust to open myself up,' he said.
The Duke, who in his book Spare admitted taking a number of illegal drugs in his life, praised psychedelic-assisted therapy – a type of treatment that has split doctors.
Magic mushrooms, MDMA and ketamine are used to change the brain rather than treat symptoms of depression and PTSD with common anti-depressants.
He said: 'To combine conventional therapy with modern day medicines breaks down those walls and those barriers to be able to open yourself up and go deeper than you would ever dare to go.
'Psychedelic assisted therapy is no longer a fringe idea or thought. It's really becoming, I think, mainstream.'
Harry's revelations follow Meghan's return to the spotlight yesterday as the Duchess of Sussex , 45, and the Nobel Peace laureate Malala, 29, were photographed leaving the luxury hotel together in Mayfair before sharing a warm hug outside the foyer.
Meghan was wearing a camel Tove Studio coat worth £1,695, a £630 cashmere sweater in wheat by LA-based label CO and Ralph Lauren's £1,700 white satin Charmaine trousers.

articles.title_orig: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.title_zh: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.content_orig:
Singapore, one of the wealthiest cities in the world, has become the most polluted on the planet as it chokes under a blanket of thick, toxic smog caused by fires in neighboring Indonesia.
Pollution has cast a pall on the city-state as it gets ready to host a packed weekend of marquee events ranging from international conferences to the glitzy Formula One Grand Prix night race.
Air quality in the city-state was at the “very unhealthy” range with an air quality index (AQI) of 216 Friday mid-morning, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir.
The financial hub topped the list of most polluted cities by IQAir this week and was still at the top spot Friday morning. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected by the Indonesian fires, was at number two.
Singapore’s skyline, including Marina Bay Sands and other skyscrapers were reduced to faint silhouettes amid the pollution.
The key Asian financial hub – with a population of 6.21 million and annual GDP of more than $650 billion – and neighboring Malaysia have had to endure the haze almost annually.
Fires in Indonesia are an annual event during the country’s dry season when huge stretches of peatland are cleared and drained for commercial plantations, including those that produce palm oil, an ingredient used in a slew of products from noodles to toothpaste.
But this year, the arrival of what’s expected to be a “super” El Niño — a supercharged version of the natural climate pattern which tends to bring bone dry conditions to the country — has set the stage for unusually intense blazes.
In an update on its website Thursday, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said “moderate to dense smoke plumes from southern and central Sumatra and West Kalimantan were observed to drift towards Singapore,” referring to Indonesian regions.
“Under the prevailing southeasterly or southerly winds, smoke haze may continue to drift towards Singapore,” it added.
Entertainment events held outdoors at the F1 event in Singapore could potentially be affected but not the race itself, the motorsport’s governing FIA said Thursday, according to Reuters. On Friday, race organizer Singapore GP told CNN “there are currently no plans to modify our entertainment activities” at the event.
Acts to entertain F1 spectators include Janet Jackson and The Killers, among others.
This is not the first time the Singapore night race is facing air quality issues. The races in 2015 and 2019 were also enveloped in thick haze and they went ahead.
Nevertheless, the Singapore Tourism Board told CNN on Friday: “Action plans are in place based on the intensity of the haze.”
F1 drivers, however, don’t seem too bothered. Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas, who cycled more than 400km (248 miles) from Malaysia to Singapore this week, told Reuters: “I don’t feel like it’s that extreme yet. I mean, it’s not great, but I don’t think there’s that much you can do.”
Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton told Reuters he has “much bigger issues to focus on.”
Neighboring Malaysia has also been heavily affected by the smog with the education ministry shutting schools across several states this week as the situation worsens.
