articles.title_orig: Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
articles.title_zh: Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
articles.content_orig:
FILE - This undated photo provided by the Bell County Sheriff's Department shows former Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan. Uncredited/Bell County Sheriff's Department/via AP hide caption
WASHINGTON — The firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, the Pentagon said Thursday, a stunning revelation about plans for the first military execution in more than 65 years after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had described it as being "public."
The Army announced this week that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3 after Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice on Wednesday, said, "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public." Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed and that more details would follow.
The revelation from Hegseth about the public nature of the execution — let alone one as violent as a firing squad — has raised further questions about how the death penalty is carried out in the U.S., especially after the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
"It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions," said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process "much more transparent" and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when Pike's botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.
"I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it's happening," she said.
When many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are coming to be seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice.
"Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner," he said. "I don't think that's what's motivating this. There's a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasize — the 'lethality culture.'"
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth's announcement raises a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
Though there has been long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, "I don't recall a situation in which it was instigated by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what is the motivation of the government," she said.
"This is a president who's about spectacle and that's, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver," Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
Trump, who approved Hasan's execution, has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action that preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran on Feb. 28.
"We've been told that the killing in Iran is stopping," Trump told reporters on Jan. 14. "It's stopping, and there's no plan for executions."
In his State of the Union address just days before launching the Iran war, Trump reiterated, "We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence."
The White House on Thursday referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.
Hegseth was asked Wednesday if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration. The Pentagon chief replied: "Don't care. We'll see him on Dec. 3."
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behavior at trial, he may not want to.
After firing his lawyers and representing himself, Hasan began his portion of the trial by telling jurors he was the gunman. He said little else over the next three weeks, which convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan's only goal was to get a death sentence.
The military called nearly 90 witnesses, but Hasan rested his case without calling a single person to testify in his defense and made no closing argument. Yet he leaked documents during the trial to journalists that revealed him telling military mental health workers that he could " still be a martyr " if executed.
Attorney John Galligan, a former military judge who had represented Hasan in several civil matters following his criminal trial, spoke with Hasan on Wednesday but is barred from offering much detail about that conversation. He is not representing Hasan in his criminal case but said he's worried about his physical health under the plan laid out by officials, and that Hasan has not yet had access to legal counsel.
Galligan said that according to Hasan, the commandant of the facility brought a chaplain but no attorney from either the Trial Defense Service or from his civilian defense when he was notified that Trump had signed off on his execution. Galligan called that a breach of Army regulations.
A spokeswoman for the Army said Thursday that multiple attempts were made to contact Trial Defense Service attorneys, saying they made every reasonable effort and adhered to policy.
"The civilian counsel was not reasonably available to be physically present for the notification on the 5th," the spokeswoman said, adding that counsel was located in Virginia but did not provide a name.
The spokeswoman also said Hasan has not been kept from contacting and communicating with his counsel.
Hegseth said the military hasn't executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
Amnesty International said in its report on executions in 2025 that it knew of at least 17 public executions — 11 in Iran and 6 in Afghanistan.

articles.title_zh: Oxford Area High School closed Friday after confirmed case of measles
articles.content_orig:
OXFORD, Pa. (WPVI) -- The Oxford Area High School in Chester County will be closed Friday after a confirmed case of measles was identified within the school community.
The school district announced the closure in a letter sent to families Thursday.
"We understand that news like this may be concerning for families," the district wrote. "The health and well-being of our students, staff and community are incredibly important to us, and we recognize that receiving this information can raise questions, concerns and uncertainty."
READ MORE | Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania amid the state's largest outbreak in decades
School officials said the Chester County Health Department will contact anyone believed to have been exposed.
The announcement comes as Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases , with 86 cases reported in Chester County.
Earlier this week, Jeanne Franklin, director of the Chester County Health Department, said officials had been working closely with school nurses and superintendents ahead of the school year because of concerns about measles transmission.
According to the district's letter, anyone who is not vaccinated against measles, or cannot provide proof of vaccination, must stay away from school and school-related activities for 21 days following a potential exposure.
Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through the air or direct contact.
Early symptoms include cough, runny nose, fever as high as 104 Fahrenheit and red, watery eyes, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Two to three days after symptoms start, patients may develop Koplik spots, which are tiny white spots that may appear inside the mouth on the inner cheek.
Three to five days after symptoms start, patients may experience a rash, first appearing on the face at the hairline before moving downwards to the neck, chest, stomach, arms, legs and feet. Fever may spike even higher than 104 F when the rash appears, the CDC says.
The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection, and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says.

articles.title_orig: Plymouth skateboarder heading to World Skate Games aged 60
articles.title_zh: Plymouth skateboarder heading to World Skate Games aged 60
articles.content_orig:
An amateur skateboarder is set to represent his country for the first time almost 50 years after he took up the sport.
Darren Miles, 60, from Plymouth, is to represent Great Britain in the slalom event at the World Skate Games in Paraguay later this month.
Miles will take part in three disciplines as part of the team made up of a mixture of professionals and amateurs.
"When I was 10 I never thought I would be skateboarding at 60 for my country so that's the main attraction," he said.
Miles first became interested in the sport in 1977 in Norfolk where he "always had a skateboard and always skated around".
In 2020 he "realised he was slowly losing his tricks" and took to slalom, which involves speed skateboarding around cones.
When he heads to the World Skate Games, Miles said he could be up against competitors who are in their 20s as well as those his own age.
He said "to finish and not get disqualified" would be a successful games for him.
"There's a top 16, I don't really anticipate getting into there, but I'll be going there and supporting all the other guys that are racing, because a few of the English guys are in with a good chance," he said.
"I'll be supporting them and just enjoying being at the event."
He said he enjoyed travelling for skateboarding events and the social aspect of the sport was a "big draw" for him.
"Sometimes you get a sport that's what matches your personality and it can be a lot of fun with a shared danger," he said.
"Everybody's been really supportive and I think a little bit amazed."

articles.title_zh: Key takeaways from US Senate debate in Michigan between El-Sayed, Rogers
articles.content_orig:
The leading candidates in Michigan’s heated Senate race have faced off in their first televised debate, with less than a month remaining before the United States midterm elections.
Thursday’s hour-long debate was a microcosm of how tense the toss-up race has become.
Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, formerly the health director for Wayne County, repeatedly sought to paint his Republican adversary Mike Rogers as a yacht-owning millionaire out of touch with ordinary voters.
For his part, Rogers, a former member of the US House of Representatives, lobbed accusations at El-Sayed that he was soft on “terrorism” and had foreign sympathies.
The Michigan-born El-Sayed has repeatedly faced Islamophobic attacks while on the campaign trail, with Republican President Donald Trump labelling him an “extremist, terrorist sympathizer” whose history “goes back to the days of the Jihad”. If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate.
The two candidates spent much of their hour onstage together speaking over one another, as they exchanged pointed barbs.
“He can’t condemn a terrorist act that happened on our soil in the state of Michigan. He can’t bring himself to condemn –,” Rogers began, referencing a March attack on a synagogue.
“I did condemn it,” El-Sayed said, jumping in. “No, you did not,” Rogers replied, with El-Sayed quickly responding, “You make stuff up. You make stuff up.”
The Senate race in Michigan is considered key to the battle for control of the US Senate. Democrats are seeking to flip both chambers of Congress, but shifting control of the Senate will be a tougher prospect, given that only a third of its 100 seats are on the November 3 ballot.
Host Rick Albin at times struggled to keep the debate on track, as tensions rose.
“We’ve got dozens of questions we want to get to. You can’t litigate all of these with 14 different rebuttals, so please work with me,” Albin told the two candidates at one point.
Here are the key takeaways from the evening’s debate.
The ferocity of the debate was underscored by the high volume of ad hominem attacks the candidates deployed against each other.
But Rogers repeatedly pushed a series of attacks that seemed to centre on El-Sayed’s identity as a Muslim.
In response to a question about healthcare, Rogers said that El-Sayed has “taken money from individuals on his campaign who openly support Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaeda”.
Later, when asked about his position on surveillance by Flock cameras, Rogers argued that such technology has helped catch people suspected of terrorism. He then implied that El-Sayed’s concerns about the cameras were suggestive.
“Why would that bother you?” Rogers asked El-Sayed. “Well, if you have somebody in your family that might be on the terrorism watch list …”
El-Sayed interjected, seeming to dare Rogers to continue his thought.
“Are you going to go ahead and say that I’m a – go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing about it the whole time. Just say it. Just say it. Go ahead and say it.”
Muslim and Arab candidates in the US have frequently been subjected to Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail, accusing them of support for “terrorism” and Islamic fundamentalism.
There were issues, however, on which both candidates found a measure of common ground.
Both Rogers and El-Sayed agreed the US-Israeli war against Iran should end, but they had opposite views on Washington’s relationship with Israel and its role in the conflict.
High gasoline prices and inflation, El-Sayed said, were directly caused by the Iran war, and he blamed the Trump administration for Iran’s decision to shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a critical trade route.
“This is what happens when you start wars you never should be fighting,” El-Sayed said. “We literally taught the Iranian regime that they have a choke on the Strait of Hormuz, and now we’re living in that reality.”
Rogers agreed that “we need [the war] to come to an end”, but he also justified the conflict, saying that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been “set back twenty years”, echoing a frequent White House talking point.
The Trump administration has argued that the war was necessary to prevent Iran from creating a nuclear weapon, a goal Tehran has long denied.
Rogers’s position led El-Sayed to accuse him of “cheerleading” for the war and the Trump administration.
As part of the debate about US foreign policy, the candidates were also pressed on their positions about the US alliance with Israel.
The country is considered the largest overall recipient of US aid since World War II. From the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023 through September 2025, experts estimate that Israel received nearly $21.7bn in military aid.
El-Sayed has openly called for ending aid to Israel, and he has repeatedly denounced the conflict in Gaza as a genocide, in line with evaluations from United Nations experts and human rights watchdogs.
During the debate, he indicated he preferred US taxpayer dollars to be spent on domestic concerns like education and healthcare, rather than Israeli aid.
“He wants unconditional support for a foreign government,” El-Sayed said of Rogers. “I want unconditional support for kids in our schools, unconditional support for our healthcare, childcare.”
He also blamed Israel for the US military action in Iran. “I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in war with Iran,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers, meanwhile, has joined most of his fellow Republicans in continuing to support aid for Israel. He argued that the country had “the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood”.
“Is there anything Israel could do that would lose your support?” the debate host asked.
“Listen, if they’re talking about using nuclear weapons, they would definitely lose my support,” Rogers replied.
Another hot-button issue during the debate was Trump’s crackdown on immigration.
The Republican leader has pledged to carry out the largest mass deportation effort in US history, and his campaign has spurred human rights concerns.
When asked how they would approach the crackdown, both Rogers and El-Sayed agreed on tempering the militarised nature of the campaign.
In several cities, including Minneapolis, Minnesota, immigration authorities have been accused of racial profiling and using excessive force against immigrants and protesters, as well as violating their rights to due process.
Multiple fatal shootings have occurred during immigration enforcement operations, including the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.
Rogers indicated he would not have supported such confrontational operations, but he repeated a Trump claim that the raids were taking dangerous criminals off the streets.
“I think the public efforts in Minnesota were probably not appropriate,” Rogers said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighbourhood for less problems. So that, to me, was something that they could have done differently.”
He later claimed that, under Trump, the country had seen “the largest decrease in murders ever recorded”.
El-Sayed, meanwhile, has previously voiced support for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a key agency in Trump’s deportation campaign. He defended that stance on the debate stage.
“ICE right now is not about immigration enforcement. ICE is about terrorising our streets,” he said.
Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada, felt acutely in neighbouring Michigan, was another key topic of conversation.
El-Sayed depicted Rogers as an uncritical backer of Trump and his tariffs and tied him to past free trade deals such as the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), which paved the way for companies to shift manufacturing facilities out of the US – though Rogers did not enter Congress until 2001, eight years after NAFTA passed.
“You did that, man. That was your policy. NAFTA, that was your policy,” said El-Sayed.

articles.title_orig: European and World Day against the Death Penalty, 10 October 2026: Joint statement by the High Representative of the European Union and the Secretary General of the Council of Europe
articles.title_zh: European and World Day against the Death Penalty, 10 October 2026: Joint statement by the High Representative of the European Union and the Secretary General of the Council of Europe
articles.content_orig:
European and World Day against the Death Penalty, 10 October 2026: Joint statement by the High Representative of the European Union and the Secretary General of the Council of Europe
The European Union and the Council of Europe are unequivocally opposed to the death penalty, in all cases and in all circumstances.
Progress towards the global abolition continued over the past year. Lebanon abolished the death penalty in August 2026. The Gambia and Vietnam reduced the number of crimes punishable by death and Sierra Leone ratified the second optional protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, ruling out execution within the jurisdiction of the State Party. Cambodia, the Central African Republic and Chad all took steps towards ratification. These examples serve as a reminder that change is always possible.
Only 17 countries are known to have carried out executions in 2025, but the sharp increase of executions is alarming. Recorded executions have risen by 78% compared with 2024. Most took place in Iran but there were significant increases in Egypt, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Singapore and Yemen. Executions continued in the United States. Owing to state secrecy, the executions carried out in China are not reflected in global statistics because of state secrecy, although it is estimated that thousands of death sentences were carried out in the country last year. Belarus remains the only country in Europe applying the death penalty.
Moreover, the continued use of the death penalty for drug-related offences is particularly concerning. Under international human rights law, capital punishment is restricted to the most serious crimes, understood as crimes of extreme gravity involving intentional killing. Using the death penalty to punish drug production and trafficking does not meet this threshold, nor is it effective. Evidence shows it does not deter crime better than other sentences. The death penalty also removes any hope of rehabilitation and will always carry the risk of fatal miscarriages of justice.
On this European and World Day against the Death Penalty, the European Union and the Council of Europe call on all States that retain the death penalty to immediately establish a moratorium on executions as a first step towards abolition. A moratorium should lead to existing death sentences being commuted and the full compliance with international human rights law and standards, pending abolition.
The European Union and the Council of Europe remain resolute in opposing any attempt to reintroduce or expand the death penalty, including in Europe. Alongside international partners, civil society, and legal professionals, we will continue to promote democratic debate grounded in human rights and the rule of law, with the goal of achieving universal abolition. In this respect, the recent World Congress against the death penalty in France demonstrated the pivotal role that the judiciary can play in abolition, as well as the importance of engaging young people. We welcome Morocco’s decision to host the 10th World Congress in 2029.
The death penalty—including the process leading to execution—constitutes inhumane and degrading treatment. We call on all States to embrace restorative justice and join the growing global movement rejecting capital punishment.

articles.content_orig:
October 8, 2026 at 11:47 pm
The season’s winningest driver adds another to his tally with a strong performance in Ohio
Michael “Buddy” Kofoid hit the entire field with a knockout punch Thursday night.
The World of Outlaws NOS Energy Drink Sprint Car Series rolled into Findlay, OH’s Millstream Speedway to kickoff Sheldon Haudenschild ’s NOS Energy Drink Buckeye Brawl Weekend . A stout field of 39 cars checked in, and Kofoid put a beatdown on them all in the Roth Motorsports No. 83.
The Penngrove, CA native rocketed out to the early advantage after starting on the pole for the 30-lapper. David Gravel settled into second and began to regain some ground on Kofoid as lapped traffic became a factor.
But late caution flags continued to clear the path ahead for Kofoid by giving him clean air. Garet Williamson ripped by Gravel late for second, but he also couldn’t pose a threat to Kofoid as the laps faded away. Kofoid took the checkered flag with more than a second advantage to claim round one of the three-round brawl.
“That whole race I could keep the car wherever I wanted it to be,” Kofoid said. “If I needed to pull out of line, I could do something good with it. It’s just a testament to how talented Dylan (Buswell) is as well as Nate (Knotts), and Peyton (Friedrich). They do an extremely good job. I’m very thankful to have them in my corner.”
Kofoid added to his Series-leading win total in 2026 with his 15th of the campaign. That also moved he and the Roth Motorsports crew one checkered flag away from making team history. If they can pick up one more before the season is over, they’ll equal the winningest World of Outlaws campaign in the long history of Dennis and Teresa’s famed team. The 24-year-old took sole possession of 23rd on the all-time win list with his 37th career score.
Garet Williamson finishes runner-up in the Fischer Motorsports No. 23 to get back on the podium for the first time in roughly a month, his 11th top three of the year.
David Gravel posted yet another solid finish with a third-place effort aboard the Big Game Motorsports No. 2. That’s 30 podiums in 2026 for the two-time and defending champion.
Spencer Bayston and Parker Price-Miller rounded out the top five.
Garet Williamson grabbed the Race//Ready Hottest Lap of the Night.

Heat Races belonged to Bill Balog ( NOS Energy Drink Heat One), Buddy Kofoid (TheGreatestStoreonDirt.com Heat Two), Sheldon Haudenschild (WIX Filters Heat Three), and Garet Williamson (Golf Cart Services Heat Four).
The SPA Technique #1 Redraw went to David Gravel .
Buddy Kofoid topped the Toyota Dash.
Donny Schatz won the Micro-Lite Last Chance Showdown.
Ricky Peterson drove from 23rd to 15th to earn the KSE Racing Products Hard Charger.
Sheldon Haudenschild was the Tub O’ Towels Seventh Place Finisher.

articles.title_orig: 27th annual Bailando International Dance Festival brings dancers from around the world to Corpus Christi
articles.title_zh: 27th annual Bailando International Dance Festival brings dancers from around the world to Corpus Christi
articles.content_orig:
Making its southern hemisphere debut, Dance Reflections will feature collaborators of Rosalía, Madonna and Beyoncé – and a high-wire takeover of the Cutaway
Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email
A “once-in-a-lifetime” program of dance works of scale will be coming to Sydney in January, including 11 international works from France, Belgium, South Africa and beyond making their Australian premiere.
The program, which triples the scale of the dance offering at the last Sydney festival , will bring 174 performers and crew to Sydney, with the crowning jewel being the acclaimed French choreographer Rachid Ouramdane’s Outsider. The 2024 work features 21 dancers from the Ballet du Grand Théâtre de Genève and four elite athletes, navigating a “cat’s cradle” of high wires and slack lines, to the mesmerising, minimalist music of the avant garde composer Julius Eastman.
Outsider will be performed in a purpose-built 720-seat theatre in the recently renovated Cutaway at Barangaroo – the first time the space has been activated for theatrical performance. The venue will also host Christos Papadopoulos’s My Fierce Ignorant Step; a double bill of works by the Chinese choreographer Tao Ye with his company TAO Dance Theatre; and a new work by genre-defying collective (La)Horde, best known for their work with pop stars such as Madonna, Sam Smith and Rosalía.
Under the banner of the Sydney festival, which announces its full program on 19 October, this is the first southern hemisphere outing for Dance Reflections, an international festival funded by French jewellery maison Van Cleef and Arpels, which has previously been staged in cities such as London, New York, Hong Kong and Seoul.
“Dance Reflections has been a real gamechanger in the creation and dissemination of dance on this scale,” says the Sydney festival director, Kris Nelson, who witnessed first-hand the impact the inaugural festival had in London, where he was working at the time.
In Sydney, he says, it will be a “once-in-a-lifetime” opportunity for dance lovers, including the Australian debuts of Ouramdane, (La)Horde and the rising star Leïla Ka, who has choreographed for Beyoncé. The Belgian master Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker will return to Australia with her company Rosas, and, from Australia, there’s a brand new work from Indigenous and intercultural dance company Marrugeku.
It’s been more than a decade since Sydney’s last major dance festival, Spring Dance. Launched by the Sydney Opera House in 2009, it ran for four years and featured superstars such as Akram Khan and Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui, before being dropped in 2013 for financial reasons. At the time, the Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron described the city’s dance audience as “relatively small but passionate”.
Nelson is hoping that’s changed. “I’m not daunted,” he says, pointing to the viral popularity of dance on TikTok, and the pop cultural work of choreographers such as (La)Horde and Leïla Ka, who draw from queer club culture and street dance.
after newsletter promotion
The festival is offering 10,000 A-Reserve tickets across the program at $49, and two works will be free: Trisha Brown’s seminal Roof Piece, in the gallery spaces of the Art Gallery of NSW; and the Belgian choreographer Cassiel Gaube’s tribute to house music, Soirée d’études, in the public space at Carriageworks.
“I’m really excited because we’re presenting a massive sampler of different kinds of dance, from the super classical to the acrobatic, to clubby and queer, personality-driven dance with big characters on stage, and works where you’re watching these incredible bodies do amazing geometry,” Nelson says. “This is your chance to test it out.”

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
articles.content_orig:
Government forces’ attack raises risk of internal conflict in Ethiopia that could trigger regional war
Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.
Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.
Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said.
Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea.
In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups in Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and the neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar. Ethiopia’s military pushed back and an allied militia, the Tigray Peace Force, took over Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 4 October after the TPLF withdrew from the city.
Eritrea’s information minister, Yemane Ghebremeskel, said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.” He did not explicitly confirm or deny the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Monday: “Ethiopia stands ready to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and core national interests, while urging all regional actors to address shared challenges through constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighbourliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.”
The TPLF and Ethiopia’s government fought a brutal civil war from 2020 to 2022. Between 300,000 and 800,000 civilians died , according to British government estimates. Both sides and their allies were accused of war crimes.
Eritrea intervened on the side of Ethiopia in that conflict, after a rapprochement between the two countries in 2018, which earned Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, the 2019 Nobel peace prize .
Eritrea, which gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, has a long enmity with the TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. The two countries fought a war from 1998 to 2000.
Relations between the countries have deteriorated again in recent years. Abiy has said Ethiopia needs access to the Red Sea, and state media has claimed the country has historical rights to the Eritrean port of Assab. The US-Israeli war on Iran – leading Iran to limit shipping through the strait of Hormuz – has further raised the stakes of Red Sea access.
In its statement on Monday, Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said: “Any serious discussion of regional maritime affairs and security architecture must account for Ethiopia’s legitimate interests and its enduring connection to the Red Sea.”
Yemane said in a post on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia was “incessantly beating the drums of war and openly stating … that it will launch a war of aggression against Eritrea to acquire what it calls ‘sovereign access to the sea’ … In recent weeks, it has tried to repackage this war agenda in terms of ‘self-defence’ by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea.”
Magnus Taylor, Horn of Africa deputy director at the Crisis Group thinktank, said: “The big worry is that [Abiy] might try to solve all his problems at the same time, by invading Eritrea, possibly a regime change move and also a land grab for the Red Sea port, and also solving his problem with Tigray at the same time. It’s a very ambitious military agenda, though.”
While the full impact of the fighting on Tigrayan civilians is not clear, reports have emerged of the TPLF forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15 to fight .
“The civilians in these three regions [Tigray, Amhara and Afar] didn’t get healed from the first round of violence that was halted by the peace agreement [in 2022],” said Acled Ethiopia analyst Jalale Getachew Birru. “They just started healing recently.”
Associated Press contributed to this story

articles.title_orig: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.title_zh: Awa seeks one term in Congress: ‘I don’t care’ about world policies
articles.content_orig:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hawaii News Now interviewed U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda and state Sen. Brenton Awa, candidates for Hawaii’s 2nd Congressional District, about the Iran war, aid to Israel and immigration enforcement.
Awa said he is seeking only one term in Congress.
“I only want to go for two years, one term, and the reason is, is because I don’t care about all of those world policies and all the votes that’ll have to be taken. I’ll have to care when I am taking it,” Awa said.
Awa said he wants money spent on the Iran war and support for Israel to instead go to American families dealing with disaster.
“But my biggest focus, if we’re going to send billions of dollars to Israel or another country, my only concern is why isn’t that money coming to Hawaii,” Awa said.
Tokuda said ending the war is the best way to reduce energy costs. She opposes aid to Israel because of its treatment of Palestinians.
“It’s a genocide,” Tokuda said.
“When you take a look at the weapons they are using, it was our weapons, which is why I voted against funding weapons sales to Israel for now, because that is blood on our hands,” Tokuda said.
On immigration enforcement, Awa does not oppose mass deportation but said he believes ICE has been too violent.
“The idea is good. The way they go and carry it out, and I don’t know,” Awa said. “I’m not there on the ground, so I don’t know, but other than what I see, through you guys, the media. But when you see people dying, there is no way that that should ever happen.”
Tokuda said there will be pressure to fix immigration laws after the election.
“We absolutely have to pass some kind of meaningful bipartisan immigration reform that protects our borders, that creates legal pathways to citizenship and doesn’t result in Americans getting executed in our streets,” Tokuda said.
Awa acknowledges the odds are stacked against him in a district that has never elected a Republican, and GOP voters have been discouraged by President Trump’s unpopularity.
Awa did not have to give up his Senate seat to run for Congress and has two years remaining on his term.

articles.title_orig: Australian data centre operator pulls $5bn IPO
articles.title_zh: Australian data centre operator pulls $5bn IPO
articles.content_orig:
Australian AI data center operator Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia , has withdrawn its planned mega initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, the company said in an emailed statement to CNBC.
Firmus said its board determined that the terms of the proposed offering did not adequately reflect the strength of its business and long-term growth outlook.
"The board therefore concluded that proceeding with the offer was not in the best interests of the company and its shareholders," Firmus said in a statement. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options," it added.
Firmus had reportedly planned to raise $5 billion in its IPO, pricing shares at A$11 apiece, which would have made it the second-largest new share sale in Australia's history. The IPO valued the company at around $30.6 billion.
In August, the company announced a $2 billion funding round backed by Nvidia, Coatue Management, Blackstone and Jane Street, bringing its total equity raised over the preceding year to more than $3 billion and its valuation to over $10.5 billion.
Firmus also announced agreements with Meta last month to provide GPU computing capacity at its AI data centers in Southeast Asia, built on Nvidia's DSX platform, to support Meta's AI research, model development and training.

articles.title_orig: Second Maine Senate debate takes testy turn: 3 takeaways
articles.title_zh: Second Maine Senate debate takes testy turn: 3 takeaways
articles.content_orig:
In an often-testy Tuesday night debate, Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine touted her three-decade-long record in Congress and took aim at some Trump policies — while Democrat Troy Jackson argued Collins has failed to push back against the Trump administration.
The Maine Senate race is one of November's most closely watched contests , and could prove crucial to determining which party controls the upper chamber next year. While the state leans left, and hasn't voted for a Republican presidential candidate statewide since the 1980s, Collins' history of surviving tough reelection challenges has vexed Democrats for more than a decade. Most polls show a razor-thin race.
Collins highlighted her "knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships," including her ability to score funding for projects in Maine as chair of the influential Senate Appropriations Committee.
"I've been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers," said Collins, who is running for a sixth term in the Senate.
Collins also has a history of breaking with President Trump, criticizing his trade war with Canada and strategy in Iran , and voting against the Trump-backed One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year — themes that frequently emerged in Tuesday's debate.
Asked about Mr. Trump's suggestion that he may travel to Maine as part of a pre-election campaign swing, Collins said she doesn't expect the president to visit.
"I've heard nothing from his office, and I'm not exactly his favorite senator," she said.
But Jackson — a former state Senate president who hails from the same largely rural northern Maine county as Collins — argued that Collins has not used her power effectively to push back against Trump administration policies, and accused her of siding with the president too often.
He criticized Collins for voting to confirm Trump-nominated Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, setting the stage for the high court to overturn Roe v. Wade and allow states to ban abortion for the first time in more than 50 years.
"Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?" asked Jackson.
Collins responded that when evaluating nominees to the Supreme Court, she "always look[s] at their qualifications." She said she disagreed with the decision to overturn Roe, but added that "there's only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice" — a reference to Jackson's previous opposition to abortion.
While Collins voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut Medicaid and food stamp spending and extended a set of tax cuts from the first Trump term, Jackson repeatedly criticized the senator for voting yes on an earlier procedural measure to advance the bill, arguing she should've tried to block the legislative package.
Collins said Jackson "misrepresent[ed] the facts." She noted that she opposed the bill due to its Medicaid cuts, but argued that her decision to let the bill move forward on the Senate floor allowed her to secure a $50 billion fund for rural hospitals.
Jackson responded: "Senator Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out."
Collins also pointed to her votes to restrict Mr. Trump's power to wage war against Iran, saying the war is "not well-thought out" and noting its impact on global energy markets. Jackson criticized Collins for voting against prior Iran measures .
Both candidates were critical of Mr. Trump's tariffs on Canada, which have sparked a tit-for-tat trade war with Maine's neighbor. Collins said she is opposed to the trade war but has been "working behind the scenes" to get exemptions for goods that are key to Maine's economy or to the operations of municipal governments, like road salt.
"Canada is our friend. It should be treated as such," she said.
Jackson mocked Collins' approach as writing a "strongly worded letter."
"What about everything else?" he asked. "I mean, we can't eat road salt."
The two candidates were also deeply critical of Immigration and Customs Enforcement's conduct, after a man in Maine was fatally shot by an ICE officer during a traffic stop over the summer. Collins called it "horrific," and Jackson said he was "murdered." But they clashed over the policy response. Jackson said ICE should be "disbanded" and should not have received a surge of funding, while Collins said the agency needs "serious reforms" but needs to continue to exist.
"It needs reform, not to be abolished," Collins said.
A longtime state lawmaker, Jackson initially ran for governor. But after losing in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, Jackson was swapped in as the party's Senate candidate at the last minute after the winner of the Democratic primary, Graham Platner, dropped out amid sexual misconduct allegations. Platner has denied the allegations.
Collins took aim at Jackson's record in state politics. She argued many of the affordability challenges that have animated voters — including on energy prices and Medicaid reimbursement rates — are the result of failings by politicians in the state capital of Augusta.
She also questioned Jackson's effectiveness as a legislator, pointing to bills he introduced that were rejected in committee without Democratic support.
"If you can't find one person in your own party to vote for your bills when you were the Senate president in Maine … how do you think you're going to get things done in a closely divided Senate as the most junior senator?" Collins asked her opponent.
Jackson said Collins "doesn't understand the legislative process," saying it "gums the system up" to have "one or two people vote for a bill that's not going to make it."

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike's health has seen 'profound turnaround' in last three days, lawyers say
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike's health has seen 'profound turnaround' in last three days, lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike has made a "profound" turnaround after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.
In a statement on Thursday, Pike's lawyers described her recovery as "remarkable" and said she is able to walk with assistance and is eating. She has also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution, they said.
"Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said.
The case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
"Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team said.
Pike's lawyers said they do not know the full emotional and psychological toll of the execution attempt or how long it will take her to recover.
They added that while she struggles to process what happened, she "continues to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim Colleen Slemmer".
Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
A court has ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
On Wednesday, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, such as packaging, inserts and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition before, during and after the failed execution.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions for the rest of the year and said he wants answers about what went wrong.
Pike's lawyers have called on the governor to downgrade Pike's punishment to life in prison without parole.
Proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different method to put her to death.

articles.title_orig: World Octopus Day: new discoveries about the world’s smartest invertebrates
articles.title_zh: World Octopus Day: new discoveries about the world’s smartest invertebrates
articles.content_orig:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.
Happy World Octopus Day!  Every Oct 8, the world celebrates one of the more unusual creatures of the sea. Octopuses are well-known for their eight legs and ability to squirt ink when frightened. They’ve also been known to use tools, a sign of intelligence, and can shape-shift to mimic the colors and texture of their surroundings, an effective way to disappear from both predators and prey.
Mongabay has reported on several octopus discoveries this year, including:
Ancient octopus were apex predators
Modern colossal squid are believed to be the largest invertebrates in the sea, but Mongabay’s Shanna Hanbury recently reported on an even larger ancient octopus species whose fossils were described by Japanese researchers in April 2026.
The Japanese team found a fossilized jawbone from the now-extinct Nanaimoteuthis haggarti. Based on its jaw size, researchers suggest the octopus may have reached 6.6 to 18.6 meters (22 to 61 feet) in length. On the higher end, that’s around two-thirds the size of an adult blue whale, the largest animal to ever exist.
“It suggests that it may have been among the largest invertebrates ever known,” study co-author Yasuhiro Iba, a paleontologist at Hokkaido University in Japan, told Mongabay by email.
They were likely gigantic predators that roamed the late Cretaceous seas between 100 million to 72 million years ago.
A rare look at baby octopuses
From long dead octopus to newly born, Hanbury also reported on baby Argentine octopuses and a rare photo of them.
Patagonian octopus eggs in Puerto Lobos Protected Natural Area in Argentina. Image courtesy of Martin Brogger.
These eggs belong to a small Patagonian octopus ( Octopus tehuelchus ). It’s one of the more common octopus species in the region, but researchers still haven’t been able to determine its global conservation status, although reported catches in Patagonia have declined over the past 50 years.
The black dots inside each egg are the developing eyes of the embryos, indicating that they’re progressing toward hatching. The female octopus of this species often lays her eggs in the shell of an oyster , then guards them fiercely. She even stops eating during this period.
New octopus species are described often , including a blue octopus about the size of a golf ball recently discovered in the Galapagos.
On a deep-sea expedition in 2015, scientists used a remotely operated vehicle to find a golf-ball sized, short-armed blue octopus. In a recent study , they confirmed that it’s new to science, reported Mongabay’s David Brown.
However, questions remain about how the new species, Microeledone galapagensis , makes use of its stubby arms.
“If you gather prey by moving your arms through the sediment (as we think they do), wouldn’t it be better to have longer arms with more suckers than short little arms?” queried lead author Janet Voight.
Banner image: Big blue octopus ( Octopus cyanea ) with a diver in background. Image courtesy of David Fleetham/WWF via naturepl.com.

Thursday, it's participating in "Conversations on a Bench", a 24-hour livestream event.
Ministry CEO’s will spend 24 hours sitting on a bench engaging in conversations with anyone who stops by.
The idea is to re-humanize homelessness and amplify stories of hope and transformation.

articles.title_orig: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.title_zh: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
articles.content_orig:
Military families admit ‘mixed emotions’ as aircraft carrier finally returns to San Diego after fraught stretch at sea that took severe toll
USS Lincoln arrives at San Diego base – live updates
By 4am on Thursday, the sky still pitch black, 19-year-old Pvt Grayden Monroe and his mom had already arrived to the naval base in San Diego, California . As the very first military family members to get there, they huddled on a set of metal bleachers overlooking the dark water. The duo were waiting for Monroe’s 21-year-old sister to step off the USS Abraham Lincoln, the embattled aircraft carrier that’s been at sea for the better part of a year.
Monroe, a soldier stationed at Fort Campbell, was wearing his army uniform for the occasion. “I hope she’s proud of me,” he said of his sister, “and I hope she knows damn well that I’m just as proud of her.”
As the sun rose over Naval Air Station North Island, thousands of people flooded on to the base for the USS Lincoln’s long-awaited return. The atmosphere was like a de facto festival, with a live band, performers on stilts, therapy dogs, handmade signs, giant cutouts of sailors’ smiling faces. People cried, laughed, screamed with joy.
When the Lincoln appeared in the middle distance around noon, rounding the corner past downtown, cheers erupted from around the bay. Sailors flanked the edges of the ship in uniform, waving to the crowd and making phone calls to loved ones. Below American-flag bunting, rust stains were visible on the sides of the carrier. The massive, city-like ship had finally reached land.
Military families and friends had longed for this moment for months.
The Lincoln first left San Diego last November, with an expected return date sometime in the spring. But as the US and Israel launched a war with Iran, the aircraft carrier was diverted to the Middle East , extending the deployment for the roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard for a then-unknown amount of time. The Lincoln’s deployment ended up spanning 321 days, including 264 consecutive days at sea without a port call, a record in modern naval history, the Department of Defense said .
For months, sailors have reported hazardous living conditions onboard the Lincoln: shortages of food and basic supplies, a spate of suicide attempts and a general sense of deteriorating mental health and declining morale. The reports immediately set off a political firestorm, with Democratic lawmakers calling for an investigation , even as Donald Trump and the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth , sought to downplay the situation. The US navy confirmed last month that eight service members from the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group had attempted suicide since the start of the deployment.
After the Lincoln’s return home was officially announced in August, it took the carrier almost two long months to get back to San Diego, making a brief port call in Thailand and then tracing a route east across the Pacific Ocean.
But on the naval base on Thursday, the scene wasn’t completely euphoric.
An infant in a stroller was positioned with a sign that read “I have waited 234 days to hug my daddy!” The baby’s mom, Brenda Rivas, said she was five months pregnant when her husband deployed. He missed the birth, and the first time he was able to see his daughter over a video call was six months later.
“It’s mixed emotions,” Rivas said. “I’m more sad than excited because he did miss so much.”
And an emotional reunion on the pier wasn’t in the cards for everyone, especially for the many military families that are spread across the country.
Dawn, a mother who requested that only her first name be used because she feared retaliation from military officials, anxiously watched a live feed of the ship’s arrival from a small town in Texas, her eyes “glued to the TV” for hours. Her son is a service member on the Lincoln.
“I couldn’t sleep. Tossed and turned,” she texted early on Thursday morning. “I’m feeling so happy for my granddaughter to see her daddy!”
Imagining that the scene in San Diego would be too chaotic, Dawn is instead flying to California next week to reunite with her son and his five-year-old daughter. She’s planning to help him “get everything back in order”: make sure his house is clean, whip up some home-cooked meals.
Over the past 11 months, one thing has been keeping her son sane and tethered to a reality off the ship, she said.
“He said that all he could think about was his daughter,” she said. “That’s what got him through all this.”
As the sailors floated around the globe for the past year, their relatives sat at home and waited, wondering what could be happening thousands of miles away on the ship.
Dawn’s son sent her updates via WhatsApp whenever he got service. This past spring, he told her the conditions were dire.
“Like 3rd world …” he wrote in a message. “We couldn’t get soap or toothpaste.”
He sent her pictures of mold dripping down the walls, of dwindling daily rations: sectioned cafeteria trays with only a few of the compartments full. Two hard-boiled eggs and watery soap. A scoop of grits and a few limp noodles.
The extended deployment, long working hours and supply shortages seemed to be taking their toll across the ship, especially on the younger sailors, Dawn said. Nearly half of all active-duty military members are 25 years old or younger . She could imagine her son, who’s now in his 30s, being like a father figure to some who were really struggling. The reports of some sailors attempting to jump overboard were true, her son told her.
“My son’s a tough kid, so he could take it,” she said during a phone interview last week. “But for those 19-year-old kids that go on a first deployment, it’s scary for them.”
One of the worst parts for Dawn was the unsolicited commentary, on Facebook and Instagram and in real life, saying that even if the ship’s conditions were rough, the sailors probably just couldn’t hack it.
“That’s exactly what people were saying about the people in the military: that they’re babies, and that back in 1969, or whenever they were [serving], it wasn’t like that,” she said. “I couldn’t even read the comments. I’m still upset about it.”
Those sentiments even came from Trump, who told reporters this summer that Lincoln’s deployment was “ not nearly long enough ”.
That type of remark changed everything about how Dawn viewed the president.
“I like President Trump. I voted for him. But I don’t really think he understands,” she said.
“Let his son be out there, just for a couple days, and see how it goes. If he really would tolerate that, if his son could really take it – I’m sure he couldn’t.”
In a brief press conference on the naval base Thursday, Capt Daniel Keeler, the commanding officer of the Lincoln, answered several questions from journalists about the consistent reports of poor conditions on the ship.
“[Most of those issues] occurred in March and April, while we were engaged in active combat operations against a very determined foe,” he said. “Immediately once combat operations started, we were, I would say, a little bit challenged to get the normal fill of things. But I had enough food, I had all the supplies I needed to conduct combat. We never missed a mission. I also never missed a meal.”
Meanwhile, Hegseth again played down those same issues on Wednesday, saying instead that “a few folks in the media” aimed to “turn” the ship’s deployment “into some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.
Keeler focused most of his comments this week on the success of the mission.
“For most of my sailors, this was their first time away from home, their first deployment, their first experience with combat,” he said. “I understand the anxiety that might have caused, but I can tell you this: our team of professionals on the ship led every single one of those sailors through that experience. And the great majority responded how sailors always do, with honor, courage and commitment.”

articles.title_orig: World’s largest wildlife crossing is on track to open this winter — unless El Niño intervenes
articles.title_zh: World’s largest wildlife crossing is on track to open this winter — unless El Niño intervenes
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The world’s largest wildlife crossing over the 101 Freeway in Agoura Hills is barreling toward a Dec. 2 completion date . Perhaps the only thing that could stop it is a fierce winter storm.
Already, a concrete bridge stretches across 10 lanes of whizzing traffic. Atop that, there’s a lush landscape sewn with 6,000 native plants. Recently, crews completed another overpass over adjacent Agoura Road. A big remaining to-do is to fill in the gap between the freeway and the road — and the freeway to the land to the north — with millions of cubic feet of soil to create a seamless pathway for animals.
The idea behind the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing is to provide a lifeline for mountain lions in the Santa Monica Mountains, locked in by traffic and suffering from the effects of inbreeding.
“We’re just hoping El Niño ‘s on our side,” said Beth Pratt, president of the Wildlife Crossing Fund and public face of the project. “I keep saying, ‘Mother Nature, we’re trying to help you. Let’s not throw any more complications our way.’” A super-sized version of the climate pattern is looming, and there’s a good chance Southern California could be doused.
Some rain is not a big deal but flooding would shut down work for safety reasons. At a final construction update held near the crossing Thursday, Robert Rock, lead landscape architect and principal designer for the crossing, explained that the soil in the area is rich in clay and silt. When wet, it gets dangerously slick and slippery.
Heavy precipitation can also derail the soil compaction process, where crews lay down the soil in layers and go over each with a construction vehicle known as a roller. In the distance, workers were busy doing just that as the fierce late morning sun beat down.
“If you’re trying to compact a mud puddle, it wouldn’t really compact, right?” he said at a trailhead off of Agoura Road. “Because if you push that down, the mud just [splats] in either direction.”
In fact, something like that happened amid historic rains in the winter of 2022-23. Construction workers were busy preparing to pour the concrete for the bottom layer of the north wall. But water collected in the trench that was dug for it as they were working to compact the soil.
That pushed back the original completion date of late 2025. Right-wing pundits and politicos in recent months have attacked the project over the delays and a high price tag that’s currently $114 million. A March post in an outlet published by a conservative think tank called it a “bridge to nowhere” and “jobs program for environmentalists.” U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy compared it with the state’s long-delayed, budget-busting high-speed train.
Around the time the outrage reached a fever pitch, however, the completion date was announced.
Pratt said “the hate” has worn on her. She’s been called a “fraud,” “retard” and worse, and she’s even afraid to post about the crossing on social media. “Of course we’re still going to celebrate” at the finish line, she said.
At stake is the survival of the Santa Monica Mountains’ isolated, beleaguered mountain lion population, which is listed as threatened. Seth Riley, wildlife branch chief for the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area, said 41% of documented matings were between close relatives since 2002, the start of an ongoing study of mountain lions in and around the Santa Monicas.
Just a few months ago, the National Park Service caught a young collared male at the western end of the mountain range who had a kinked tail — a sign of inbreeding. It’s not the first such documented deformity but shows the problems persist, Riley said. If the situation gets to the point where their reproduction is affected, modeling has shown there’s “essentially a 100% chance of extinction” within 50 years, he added.
But he doesn’t think it’s too late. The soon-to-open crossing will let the big cats seek mates in the Simi Hills and beyond — and allow fresh blood to travel into their neck of the woods, he said. Genetic diversity is expected to go up, though not overnight.
In the last three weeks, a trail camera stationed close to the south end of the crossing has captured coyotes, deer, a female lion with two big cubs — even as construction churns on next door, said Jeff Sikich, a wildlife biologist at the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
Recently, in the Simi Hills north of the crossing, his team marked three kittens, the first litter for the 3 ½-year-old lion known as P-113.
“These kittens might be — once they grow up and leave mom at roughly around 1½ — one of the first lions to actually use the wildlife crossing,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Aspen One begins work on world’s first battery-backed chairlift
articles.title_zh: Aspen One begins work on world’s first battery-backed chairlift
articles.content_orig:
Aspen One announced their plans at Wednesday’s annual Afternoon Blend event to make history with the introduction of the world’s first battery-backed chairlift on Snowmass Mountain.
The first phase of the installation happened on Wednesday.
“There are over 4,000 ski lifts in the world,” said Chris Miller, senior vice president of sustainability at Aspen One. “We are doing something for the first time here at Snowmass.”
Following a successful season with the new Elk Camp high-speed six-pack lift at Snowmass, Aspen One is now looking to replace the 1,250 kilowatt diesel generator with a 900 kilowatt battery backup, avoiding approximately 144 tons of carbon dioxide emissions each year going forward.
“We really do set the standard for resort operations in our industry, from a guest experience but also from a sustainability perspective,” Miller said. “Having an impact in the work that we do is super important.”
Every summer, fuel for lifts is pumped out of diesel tanks at the top of Snowmass, with trucks routinely making trips up and down the mountainside for fuel replacement, according to Miller.
“It’s bad from an environmental perspective, and you just don’t want to be moving that stuff up and down the mountains,” he added.
According to him, the new battery backup will be quieter and cleaner than the current generator as well as be charged with nearly 100% clean energy from Holy Cross Energy.
What’s happening in Aspen, in one click.
Sign up for our morning newsletter at AspenTimes.com/newsletter
Part of the challenge of getting the current 92% renewable energy at Holy Cross Energy to 100% is meeting peak demand periods, Miller explained, which requires supplemental non‑renewable generation to meet consumer needs.
Clean energy will back up the lift during the day, and when the lift stops running at 4 p.m., Holy Cross Energy can pull power back into the grid to support local energy demands.
“Aspen One is really at the forefront of helping Holy Cross get to 100% clean energy with the flexibility of these clean storage systems,” said Mike Steiner, key accounts specialist at Holy Cross. “We utilize these batteries to help shave peak demand and manage our renewable energy supply.”
Steiner told The Aspen Times that Holy Cross Energy and Aspen One have aspirations to expand this battery-backed system further, and continue reaching toward cleaner energy and a more sustainable environment.
“We’re going to install this and make sure it’s fully operational and run efficiently,” he said. “We’re working with them closely on a long-term planning approach.”
The project team expects to reach full completion early next month, Miller confirmed in his presentation on Wednesday.
This spooky season, bears don’t need an invitation to trick or treat.

articles.title_orig: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.title_zh: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.content_orig:
At least 33 people were killed on Thursday when a Russian strike caused two public buses to catch fire in eastern Ukraine , local authorities said, making it the deadliest single attack this year.
Another 18 people were injured in the attack in Kramatorsk , a city in the Donetsk region, which prompted authorities there to shut down the public transport system and urge people to move to safer parts of the country.
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” said Vadym Filashkin, the head of the Donetsk regional military administration. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.”
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SES) said the Russian strike caused a fire on two buses and in the surrounding area.
Police in Donetsk said Russian drones targeted officers who were helping victims of the strike. Police were still working to identify the victims of the strike, with some bodies having to be pieced together from fragments, they said in a statement.
Footage they released of the rescue operation shows bodies strewn across the road. Drones can be seen near the scene of the strike as responders load the injured onto stretchers and into emergency vehicles.
One emergency worker can be heard asking an injured woman for her name. The woman responds weakly, “Tanya…legs, legs.” Shots can be heard ringing out and the woman is put into an emergency vehicle.
Filashkin said he had ordered the suspension of public transportation in the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk in the wake of the attack and called on civilians to move to safer areas. “I urge everyone who remains in the Donetsk region to evacuate to safer regions of Ukraine,” he said.
“Russia is bringing death to Ukrainian soil. It is striking our cities, killing our people, and multiplying its crimes every day,” added Filashkin as he offered his condolences to the families and loved ones of victims.
CNN has reached out to Russia’s defense ministry for comment.
The deadly strike comes as Ukrainian negotiators are expected to visit the US for talks on Friday and Saturday. A source familiar with the matter told CNN US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner would meet with Ukraine’s intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zelensky said in his nightly address on Thursday that the talks would last two days and that Ukraine counted on its European allies to join in.
He added Umerov and Budanov would also use the meeting to raise the issue of air defenses – a critical issue for Kyiv.
Earlier on ⁠Thursday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the war in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate and that Washington remains committed to finding a peaceful resolution to the conflict.
“We’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war ⁠that is permanent, enduring, and fair. And that’s what we’re committed to continuing to do,” Rubio said during a visit to ⁠Portugal.
Reacting to his comments, Kremlin ‌spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia agreed with Rubio that ​the Ukraine conflict was at a stalemate.
“Yes, we agree with him,” Russian state news agency RIA Novosti quoted Peskov as saying, adding it was up to diplomats to find ways of moving towards peace.
“The art of diplomacy precisely involves finding some way out that would allow ‌moving onto ⁠a peaceful track,” Peskov was quoted as telling journalists in Turkmenistan, according to Reuters on Thursday.
The past few months have been exceptionally deadly for Ukrainian civilians. Russia has been launching near daily mass aerial attacks against the country, taking advantage of Ukraine’s critical shortage of interceptors.
A mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage. In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv.
Both Kramatorsk and Sloviansk are crucial industrial cities close to the front line. Together with nearby Kostiantynivka and Druzhkivka, they form the core of Ukraine’s remaining “fortress belt” in the Donetsk region.
Kramatorsk has long served as a strategic rear point for the Ukrainian units serving along the eastern front – and as a place to which exhausted troops could retreat for a few days of rest before their next mission. But a press officer with Ukraine’s 93rd mechanized brigade told CNN last month that is no longer an option due to frequent shelling.
The fortress belt has slowly eroded over the past four and a half years. Its southernmost anchor, Kostyantynivka , has now been effectively lost as a stronghold.

Can AI safely assess patients’ needs before they step into a doctor’s office? A study led by researchers at Google and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) and published in The Lancet today, offers an encouraging first look. As Google’s first-ever publication in the main journal of The Lancet, this research marks a significant milestone.
In a real-world clinical study at BIDMC’s ambulatory primary care clinic, 98 patients consulted AMIE , our research diagnostic AI chatbot, ahead of urgent care visits. Supervising physicians monitored the interactions in real time, and not a single conversation needed to be interrupted based on predefined safety criteria. And clinicians reported that the AI summaries helped them prepare for visits in 75% of cases and influenced their approach to care in more than half. AMIE’s differential diagnoses also matched the doctors’ final diagnoses 90% of the time.
While larger clinical trials are needed to assess patient-facing AI at scale, the findings suggest the potential for AI to enhance the patient-physician relationship and ease the strain on healthcare workers. And they demonstrate meaningful progress as we push the boundaries of what’s possible for AI in science and health . Read the complete research paper in The Lancet .

On Thursday, 15 October, the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) will present its annual report International Trade Outlook for Latin America and the Caribbean 2026: The importance of modern services exports and how to promote them. According to the report, in the current landscape marked by uncertainty and geopolitical and geoeconomic tensions, trade has maintained considerable dynamism. Commercial flows of goods from Latin America and the Caribbean have been dynamic throughout 2026, and prospects for the full year are positive.

Kimberly Guilfoyle faces renewed scrutiny over her conduct as U.S. ambassador to Greece after a Donald Trump donor alleged she offered him access to administration officials in exchange for paying a $100,000 American Express bill. The allegation has prompted calls for an investigation, while her lawyer disputes the messages behind the claim.
Eric Deters, a lawyer and former congressional candidate, made the accusation during a Thursday interview with MS NOW. He said Guilfoyle approached him last year, before her Senate confirmation hearing, and offered him connections to government officials if he covered the outstanding balance. Deters called the arrangement "absolutely" a quid pro quo and said he never owed her money. Deters also called Guilfoyle a "grifter."
Messages Deters shared with The Wall Street Journal reportedly show Guilfoyle promising he would be her "Trump ride or die" if he arranged the payment. In another exchange, she allegedly urged him to stop "papering" their conversations and use Signal instead, warning that written records could jeopardize her ambassadorship.
Jesse Binnall, Guilfoyle's attorney, challenged the messages' authenticity in comments to the Journal. He also maintained that Guilfoyle was owed money for travel and speaking engagements she completed before her nomination. Deters rejected that explanation, saying he did not owe her a balance (via The Guardian ).
Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to address the latest allegations when reporters questioned him in Athens on Wednesday and Thursday. He nevertheless called Guilfoyle "a strong ambassador." Vice President JD Vance also expressed reservations about the alleged arrangement but said he "doesn't know the full details."
The dispute follows earlier reporting by The Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle invited Greek lobbyists to official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of a Greek construction and energy company. Those allegations had already drawn concern from Democratic lawmakers overseeing foreign affairs.

BREAKING: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay for her efforts to promote international law
Wall Street was buzzing Thursday about a possible merger that would amount to much more than a hill of beans.
Starbucks said it was focused on its turnaround plan after the Financial Times reported that it explored a potential deal to take over Chipotle Mexican Grill.
“Our team is laser-focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy,” Starbucks said in a statement. “We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential.”
It added that it typically doesn’t comment on what it described as “rumors and speculation” and said it looks forward to sharing its next earnings results later in October.
The FT reported that Starbucks had hired advisers in recent months to work on a takeover proposal for Chipotle. NBC News hasn’t confirmed the report.
A tie-up between the two companies would mean a massive shake-up in the restaurant industry, which is grappling with consumers’ changing their spending and eating habits.
Before the report emerged, sending shares of Chipotle higher by 6.2%, the company had a total market value of about $39 billion. For comparison, Starbucks’ market value is at more than $105 billion.
Chipotle didn’t reply to a request for comment Thursday afternoon.
A deal would also reunite Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol with the company he led before he jumped to Starbucks in 2024.
Investors appeared worried that a deal could be a distraction for Niccol and his company. Starbucks shares fell as much as 6.6% on Thursday but closed the day only slightly lower.
The company is in the midst of a wide-ranging turnaround plan engineered by Niccol, including a redesign of Starbucks stores, new service standards to speed up customers’ orders, a refreshed menu and a reboot for its rewards program.
Just weeks ago, Niccol touted the plan’s results , saying “tremendous progress” has been made. Shareholders have seen promising returns, too. For the year, Starbucks shares are up almost 11%.
That closely tracks with the S&P 500’s 13% return so far this year. Starbucks has also far outperformed the negative 6.7% return that the S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary sector has recorded this year.
Chipotle shares have sagged by more than 11% this year and more than 20% over the last 12 months.
In July, the company’s latest earnings results beat expectations, but that followed a period of slow traffic and price hikes. Those results also came alongside soaring gas prices for consumers.
“We’re seeing encouraging progress because we’re focused on the right growth drivers,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said in a statement in July . Like Starbucks, Chipotle has also revamped its rewards program and made tweaks to its menu to lure customers back.
Chipotle has also started expanding outside the U.S., with plans to open stores in Mexico, South Korea and Saudi Arabia.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
