But will existing handhelds get the tech?
It’s already possible to get AMD’s framerate-enhancing FSR 4 boost on handhelds as old as the Steam Deck — but in June, AMD reserved the right to disappoint handheld gamers by not officially bringing FSR 4 to older handhelds. Now, AMD consumer chip boss Jack Huynh says he will bring the tech to some handhelds by the end of the year.
Which handhelds? It’s still not clear if it will come to existing handhelds, or if you’ll need a new one to get it — because it comes alongside news that AMD is releasing a new FSR4-capable chip.
“We will expand the machine learning AI-based FSR4 technology, which was first introduced to existing external graphics cards, to the entire product line including APUs, gaming laptops, and handheld devices by the end of this year,” Huynh told Korean publication The Elec (via Google Translate). “We plan to respond in two directions: launching existing APUs and new product lines.”
The Elec says that means both a new APU, and a lightweight FSR4 model for APUs, are coming by year’s end. (Previously, AMD had only promised FSR4 for desktop graphics cards, not APUs bound for laptops and handhelds.) But The Elec doesn’t seem to say if that lightweight FSR4 model is coming to handhelds specifically. Perhaps it’ll require AMD’s leaked upcoming Ryzen Z3 and/or “Gainsborough” handheld chips .
Back when AMD threw a little cold water on the idea of FSR 4 for existing handhelds, exec David McAfee told Tom’s Guide that “we want to make sure the experience and the quality is right” and that AMD would need “a sufficient amount of compute within that product” for FSR 4 to make sense. Perhaps some older laptop chips will qualify, while some older handheld chips don’t.
Valve worked with AMD to bring FSR 4 to the Steam Machine ’s console-grade AMD APU, but it hasn’t yet committed to the same for the Steam Deck handhelds.
AMD didn’t immediately respond to a request to clarify Huynh’s statement.

Columbus changed the world
His journey to the Americas began an era of exchange
Christopher Columbus, depicted in a 1904 chromolithograph, led the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa Maria across the Atlantic to the Americas in 1492. (© GraphicaArtis/Getty Images)
Christopher Columbus was not the first European to reach the Americas, a feat achieved by the Vikings. What’s more, Columbus died thinking he’d arrived in known lands in Asia rather than on a different continent.
Despite misunderstanding his location, Columbus would leave a legacy arguably more important than any explorer of his time.
The Italian navigator, sailing under the flag of Spain, landed on that first voyage in what is now the Bahamas on October 12, 1492. That journey led him to greatness, as subsequent voyages by Columbus and others would develop the Western Hemisphere and connect the Eastern and Western Hemispheres in important ways.
Columbus’ 1492 voyage across the Atlantic was “one of the most important moments in world history,” says Bradley Birzer, a history professor at Hillsdale College. It began a period when the Spanish would found settlements in the Caribbean and the Portuguese would claim Brazil.
His voyages inspired others to follow, including the Italian Amerigo Vespucci, after whom “the Americas” are named.
Colonies established subsequently by European powers formed the basis of modern-day Latin America. And English settlers who arrived in North America in the early 1600s sowed the seeds of the society that would become the United States on July 4, 1776.
“We’re not here if Columbus didn’t do what he did,” says Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation, a Washington research organization.
Columbus’ explorations set the stage for what the late historian Alfred Crosby (1931–2018) calls the “Columbian exchange,” an interchange of plants and animals between the hemispheres. Crosby described the exchange as “spectacular and significant” for its effect on the future of agricultural activities and the growth and development of the modern Americas, Europe and Africa.
For example, corn, a crop native to the Americas, improved the diet of many Europeans — it was more drought-resistant and easier to grow than other vegetables. In Africa, cultivation of corn, which stores longer than other foods, facilitated the growth of states and commercial ties among various groups, according to the Encyclopedia Britannica .
Other native American crops, such as potatoes and tomatoes, became widespread in Europe and staples in Ireland and Italy, respectively.
Demand for American tobacco by Europeans provided an economic boon to the British colonies. Chocolate (made from cacao) and hot peppers from Central and South America also found their way to the Old World, a direct result of Columbus’ voyages.
On the other side of the exchange, Columbus brought horses to the Americas. The animals revolutionized life for native cultures as hunters found that riding to hunt bison was effective.
Cattle and sheep brought from Europe also became important sources of food, clothing and shelter for American tribes. As U.S. pioneers moved westward during the 19th century, cattle pulled them in covered wagons.
“All of these things just transformed North and South America,” Birzer says.

The University of Alabama is modifying several game-day operations ahead of Saturday’s football game against Georgia as severe weather and strong winds are expected to affect parts of Central Alabama.
The game remains scheduled to be played as planned at this time, but university officials are urging fans to closely monitor weather conditions and make informed decisions about travel and shelter.
The changes come as Tropical Storm Watches are in effect across much of Central Alabama amid strengthening conditions in the Gulf of Mexico. Forecasters are warning of potentially damaging winds, heavy rainfall, flash flooding and possible tornadoes over the weekend.
The National Weather Service in Birmingham has issued watches for numerous counties, including Jefferson, Shelby, Tuscaloosa, Bibb, Chilton and Talladega. Wind gusts could reach 55 mph in the Birmingham metro area, while some southern portions of the state could see gusts between 65 and 75 mph.
Those winds could down trees and power lines, block roads and cause power outages.
To reduce the risk to fans and prevent damage from the expected weather, tailgating will not be permitted on the University of Alabama campus before noon Saturday.
After noon, personal tailgating will be allowed only in uncovered areas, weather permitting.
The university said no tailgate drop-offs or setups will be allowed anywhere on campus Friday. Any tailgating supplies placed on campus before noon Saturday will be removed and discarded.
Corporate tailgating vendors, including Gameday Done Right, will not set up on the Quad because of the forecast for severe weather and high winds overnight Friday.
Fans may access the Quad and other campus gathering areas after noon, but those areas will first need to be inspected and determined to be safe. The university said there will be no Saturday tailgate supply drop-off for the Quad.
Electrical and power services will not be restored to the Quad until university officials determine conditions are safe.
The university also said it could further delay operations if weather conditions warrant.
Campus parking lots and shuttle services are currently scheduled to open at noon Saturday.
Fans attempting to park on campus before the lots officially open will be turned away. Parking pass holders who purchased parking through Clutch! will receive direct updates if conditions change.
Shuttle buses will begin operating once parking lots open, unless sustained winds cause additional delays.
Visitors using off-campus parking are encouraged to check with individual parking operators for potential schedule changes.
Several activities scheduled ahead of the game have also been canceled or modified because of the expected weather.
All activities on and around the Quad have been canceled, as have all Champions Lane activities.
The planned 8 p.m. Friday announcement at Gorgas Library celebrating the successful conclusion of the Rising Tide 2.0 capital campaign has also been canceled.
The Elephant Stomp is not currently planned.
The Walk of Champions is expected to continue approximately 2 hours before kickoff, weather permitting.
ESPN's College GameDay will be held inside Coleman Coliseum.
The north and east doors are scheduled to open at 5:30 a.m., with fans allowed to begin lining up at 5:15 a.m.
Because of the expected weather, overnight queuing and camping outside Coleman Coliseum will not be permitted.
Fans attending College GameDay should also be aware that only clear bags will be allowed inside the venue and will be inspected upon entry. The field-goal kick associated with the program will take place inside Coleman Coliseum.
University officials said weather conditions and game-day operations could continue to change as the storm system develops.
Fans are encouraged to monitor official University of Alabama News, UA Gameday and UA Safety communications, including social media and university apps, for updates concerning weather, parking, tailgating and other game-day operations.
The university said the changes are intended to help provide a safe game-day environment while weather conditions remain uncertain.

A grandmother of 12 is being credited for breaking her own Guinness World Record for a woman holding a plank move for the longest time period.
DonnaJean Wilde made her potential record-breaking attempt at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week and completed a plank hold for five hours.
Guinness World Records confirmed to ABC News that Wilde's title record, which she achieved on March 21, 2024, is 4 hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds. The organization said it has received an application for Wilde's newest record attempt and will review evidence before declaring a new record.
"I always wondered if I could have gone to five [hours]," Wilde told ABC News' Danny New of her motivation to break her own plank hold record.
According to World Senior Games, the record attempt began at 3:03 p.m. MT, with judges rotating out every hour until 8:03 p.m. MT, when WIlde's attempt ended.
"Some of them would come right down to me: 'Go, DonnaJean, go! You're doing great!'" Wilde said of the judges.
The 61-year-old -- who lives in Alberta, Canada -- said her training to prepare for her record attempt included having her 3-year-old granddaughter, Rose, lie on her back while she planked.
Wilde said she wasn't certain she would be able to accomplish her five-hour feat and even considered giving up during the attempt.
"I told [my husband] Randy, 'I'm done. I'm going down.' And they [the audience] all chanted me to the end. They got me through the last 10 minutes," Wilde said.
If her latest record attempt is recognized, Wilde would have earned her third Guinness title, following her previous plank record and her other record for the most pushups done in an hour by a woman, at 1,575.
It's another impressive feat for Wilde, who said she didn't rest for long after her latest plank feat. The morning after her record attempt, she ran in a 3,000-meter race.
As for her next record attempt, Wilde said she hopes to do at least 1,600 pushups in an hour and break her second record title.

articles.title_orig: Florida health officials meet amid fierce debate over childhood vaccine plans
articles.title_zh: Florida health officials meet amid fierce debate over childhood vaccine plans
articles.content_orig:
Heather Hazzan / Self magazine
Last month, a child in Montana died of Haemophilus influenzae type b, better known as Hib. According to the state health department, the child had not received the Hib vaccine , and Montana's four other pediatric deaths from H influenzae since 2012 were all caused by strains the vaccine doesn't cover. That makes this the state's first pediatric Hib death in at least 14 years.
Many parents have never heard of Hib, because the vaccine worked so well that the disease all but disappeared. Public health is often called a victim of its own success, and Florida's proposal could make children the victims instead.
Tomorrow, Florida's Department of Health will hold a public hearing on its plan to remove requirements for four vaccines that protect against Hib, pneumococcal disease, hepatitis B, and chickenpox. The Hib and pneumococcal vaccines are currently required for daycare and preschool, while hepatitis B and chickenpox are required through K-12.
State officials have framed the change as a matter of parental rights and "medical freedom," and the department hasn't pointed to any new evidence about the safety or effectiveness of these vaccines. The department can remove these four through its rulemaking authority, while measles and polio requirements are written into state law and would need action from the legislature.
These four vaccines also protect against the diseases parents are least likely to remember, which makes them the easiest to give up. Florida is the first state to propose this, and health departments in some other states have similar authority to try it.
Before Hib vaccines came into wide use in the late 1980s, Hib was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in American children under 5 years, and about one in 200 kids developed invasive Hib disease by age 5. Each year, roughly 20,000 young children got severe Hib disease, and about 1,000 died. Among children who survived Hib meningitis, 15% to 30% were left with hearing loss or other permanent neurologic damage.
Pediatricians who trained in that era still talk about it (and the clinicians we work with often name Hib as one of the scariest vaccine-preventable diseases). MaryAnne, who shared her story with Voices for Vaccines , nearly died of Hib at age 4 in the early 1960s, when an infection of her epiglottis left her unable to breathe and doctors performed an emergency tracheotomy.
These four vaccines also protect against the diseases parents are least likely to remember, which makes them the easiest to give up.
Once the vaccine became routine, cases in young children dropped by 99% , and in 2022 the United States recorded just 17 confirmed cases in children under 5. Provisional surveillance data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show 28 cases so far this year.
Florida pediatricians have been warning about an increase in Hib cases for months. At a state workshop on the proposal last December, a Panama City pediatrician said he had seen two unvaccinated children with Hib in the intensive care unit in the previous six months, a 4-month-old who died and a 2½-year-old left “brain dead.”
All four diseases are easy to underestimate, and for Hib, the name is part of the reason. The bacterium was first identified during an influenza outbreak in 1892, before scientists knew a virus caused the flu. The “influenzae” part of its name makes it sound like something a flu shot would cover.
Pneumococcal disease is just as unfamiliar to most parents, even though, before the vaccine, about one in 500 US 1-year-olds developed a serious invasive infection like meningitis or a bloodstream infection each year. Many adults remember chickenpox as a harmless rite of passage, even though before the vaccine it caused 10,500 to 13,500 hospitalizations and 100 to 150 deaths in this country each year. Hepatitis B tends to be thought of as an adult disease, even though about 90% of babies who become infected develop chronic infection, and about a quarter of people chronically infected during childhood eventually die early from cirrhosis or liver cancer.
When a vaccine works, the disease disappears from daily life, along with the stories and firsthand experience that once made the vaccine feel necessary. For most families, the last time anyone saw these diseases up close was a generation or more ago. Measles still has some cultural memory (and plenty of recent headlines), while most parents today have never known a child with Hib meningitis.
That gap makes it easy to frame these four shots as optional extras, and it helps explain why Florida's proposal has drawn far less public outrage than a move against the measles vaccine would.
When a vaccine works, the disease disappears from daily life, along with the stories and firsthand experience that once made the vaccine feel necessary.
Supporters point out that removing a requirement doesn't take the vaccine away, and parents can still choose it. In practice, decades of research link stronger school requirements with higher vaccination rates, and easier exemptions with higher exemption rates and more disease.
Florida is starting from a weak position, too, with kindergarten vaccination coverage falling substantially in recent years, from at least 93.5% for major required vaccines in 2019-20 to 88.9% of kindergarteners fully vaccinated in 2025-26. Requirements also prompt the pediatrician visit and records check that catch a missed dose before a child starts daycare or school.
Even with the governor's support, no Florida legislator filed a bill to repeal the state's school vaccine laws in any of its 2026 sessions, and no state has repealed its school vaccination laws outright.
But the health department route doesn't need legislators at all, and many states give their health departments authority over which vaccines are required for school (how much varies by state), which means appointed officials in those states could do what Florida's surgeon general is attempting.
Anti-vaccine advocates are already pushing Louisiana, Texas, and Idaho to follow Florida's lead. In each state, the most exposed vaccines will be the ones that aren't written into statute and that parents are least likely to defend. If Florida's rule is approved, other states with similar rules could follow the same process.
Public support for school requirements remains strong, and 81% of US parents back requiring measles and polio vaccines for school, with some exceptions, although those aren't the vaccines on the table in Florida. That support goes only so far if parents don't know what Hib, pneumococcus, hepatitis B, and chickenpox did to children before we had vaccines.
For those of us in public health and medicine, the job is to make these diseases familiar again with facts and real cases. Clinicians can share what they've seen, health departments can report cases and deaths quickly and clearly, and communicators can talk about these four vaccines with the same urgency we bring to measles.
States also need to know where coverage is slipping. Montana is the only state that doesn't require school districts to report vaccination data to its health department, and legislators voted down a bill to change that last year, just as measles returned to the state for the first time in 35 years.
Hib became a disease most parents have never heard of because vaccination made it rare. But keeping it rare means maintaining the high vaccination rates that requirements help sustain.

articles.title_orig: Overwhelmed by parenting in a world of tech? This Wisconsin doctor can help
articles.title_zh: Overwhelmed by parenting in a world of tech? This Wisconsin doctor can help
articles.content_orig:
There’s never been one right way to be a parent.
But the world has changed a lot over the last two decades. The internet, smartphones, social media and now AI have added extra challenges to the task of raising children. It can feel impossible for parents to keep up.
A Wisconsin doctor and researcher is the co-author of a new book that tries to help parents and caregivers tackle those thorny issues with practical advice backed by years of study.
WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter.
Dr. Megan Moreno is a professor of pediatrics and affiliate professor of educational psychology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Her new book is called, “ Connecting: Raising Kids in the Digital World ,” and it comes out Oct. 13.
Moreno said she hopes to empower parents.
“In a world of influencers, parents are still the first and most important influencers for kids,” Dr. Moreno said. “Kids are looking to them for these conversations and boundaries, and these can be boundaries you negotiate together.”
Dr. Moreno joined WPR’s “ Wisconsin Today ” to give some tips for parenting in a technology-focused world.
Moreno said that these days, there are a lot of judgments on parents when it comes to how they let their kids engage with technology. But like potty training, sleep training or dealing with tantrums, there are a lot of different ways to be successful.
“You need to approach it with a little bit of grace and a little bit of understanding that you might not get it right every single day, every single time,” Moreno said.
Instead of trying to meet some singular, perfect standard for parenting, Moreno encourages striving for “good enough” — embracing variation and learning from experience.
If there’s no one right way to parent around technology, how can parents decide what strategy is right for their child?
“I think a lot of it starts with curiosity. Parents can sometimes feel a little intimidated that their kids are ahead of them on their tech expertise,” Moreno said. I think it’s completely OK for parents to say, ‘What the heck is Instagram? Show me how it works.’ Or, ‘Hey, this is a new game you’re playing. Show me what you like about it.’”
Moreno said having those conversations early is important to prepare for when they might get into trouble with their online habits.
“(Then) your child knows they can come to you, and even if you’re not crazy about what they did or what they saw, you’re still there to support them,” Moreno said.
If parents want to cut down on their child’s screen time, understanding what they like about their preferred digital activity can be a great way to connect them with offline interests.
“Some parents will use that information and say, ‘Oh, you love building games online. Let’s go get some clay,’ or ‘Let’s get that pile of scrap wood that I had in the backyard and build something,” Moreno said.
As kids get older, parents can have conversations with them about the “Why?” behind technology. That might include conversations about how platforms are designed to suck them in and keep them scrolling.
“That can be really empowering for kids to feel like rebellion isn’t sneaking their phone in their bed at night — the rebellion is shutting that feed down,” Moreno said.
Encouraging digital literacy can be especially helpful if a child is engaging with online influencers — people who generate interest in something by posting about it online. Influencers may seem authentic, but kids may not understand that influencers have ulterior motives.
Parents can prompt questions like: Are they selling something? Why do you think that they’re selling it to people your age? What are they hoping you’re going to do? Where else could you be giving your time and attention?
Kids learn more from what their parents do than what they say, Moreno said. So setting a good example is important.
“If you give your kids screen time limits, but they see you late at night scrolling, they’re going to learn more from what you’re doing,” Moreno said.
But moments of imperfection can be great learning experiences for kids.
“A parent can say, ‘Oh my gosh! I got totally caught up in cute cat videos. I made a mistake. I’m going to do it differently next time,’” Moreno said. “That’s such a powerful teacher for kids.”
In the same way that there’s no one right way to parent around technology, the rules and guidance that parents give their kids should change as their child grows and changes.
“Kids interact with media in very different ways as they navigate later childhood, early adolescence and late adolescence, and being able to help them decide what they’re going to embrace and what they’re going to let go of is a really great part of parenting,” Moreno said.
That growth will be different for every kid, so parents should be flexible and adapt to what they observe in their child. Moreno heard that same idea when she asked focus groups of 10 to 14 year olds: What is the right age to get your first smartphone?
“They said it’s not about age — it’s about responsibility, it’s about maturity, and it’s about being able to respect the boundaries your parents give you,” Moreno said.
Parents can take advantage of resources like Moreno’s new book to guide how they help their kids through the digital world. Moreno also recommended online resources like The American Academy of Pediatrics Center of Excellence on Social Media and Youth Mental Health and that organization’s Family Media Plan , as well as Common Sense Media .
Moreno encouraged parents to talk with other adults about how they’re navigating technology in their households.
“Parents do that a lot when their kids are young, but less so as they get older, and I think having parents connect to each other and support each other is a really key thing that will help us with the next decade of tech use,” Moreno said.

articles.title_orig: In a world where the glamour of evil rules, Catholics must create beauty
articles.title_zh: In a world where the glamour of evil rules, Catholics must create beauty
articles.content_orig:
Think of a moment when you felt God’s nearness. And I mean felt, not as something you could explain or argue, but as a closeness that reached into the depth of your being in ways you could barely describe—and yet you knew.
My son had one of those experiences. He was on a work trip to Mexico City and took an afternoon to join a tour of the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe. He was rushed and distracted, so he decided to return later on his own. On a long-distance video call that evening, his eyes wide with wonder, he described the experience. He was sitting quietly before the image of La Virgen preserved on Juan Diego’s tilma high above the main altar when, suddenly, he “knew” he was not alone. And then it hit him all at once that he was never alone. He felt La Virgen’s loving gaze fixed intently on him and became aware that my late mother (his beloved Abi) was sitting next to him in the pew, “like every time we went to Misa together when I was little.”
The whole experience felt familiar and natural; being there with a community in prayer was being en familia. In the beauty of that moment, he discovered that heaven and earth were not separate realities but instead one. My son was changed by that moment. In a world steeped in materialist cynicism, where our young struggle with disillusionment and despair, he had an experience of beauty so profound that it generated hope in him, a hope that keeps renewing itself. When his little blind dog was sick recently, he hung a small medal of La Virgen from his collar. God’s compassion knows no limits.
Maybe you have had such an experience of beauty. I hope so, because you also represent hope.
The experience my son had was not a private revelation but the fruit of a community—the loving work of generations who recognize the primal human need for beauty and continue to labor to make it perceptible. He benefited from artists and architects who envision ways to help us feel the power of beauty. He kept in his heart the stories that mothers and grandmothers recount of God’s loving presence. Most of all, he received the gift that countless communities of faith generously bestow on one another—the witness to being grafted into a larger story and the renewal this brings from generation to generation. This recognition and expansion of beauty as heaven’s solidarity with us has been central to the Christian faith from its very beginnings.
St. John Paul II, in his pastoral “ Letter to Artists ,” in a section titled “The ‘Beauty’ That Saves,” writes: “Faced with the sacredness of life and of the human person, and before the marvels of the universe, wonder is the only appropriate attitude.” The Christian imagination is that quality that allows us to push against the boundaries and apparent inevitability of an often painful what is into the possibility and healing of what could be by the light of our religious tradition. For Christians, this open possibility is the source of our hope in God’s reign, which is both here and not yet here. The reign is both breaking in and incomplete as it pulls us toward its fulfillment. The reign requires imagination, commitment and experiences of it, perceptible in beauty, to nourish it. The invitation to imagine expansively and the work of cultivating ways to do this are central to a faith that engages with the realities of this world and responds to the “ signs of the times, ” as the Second Vatican Council emphasized.
Our theologies, the ways we speak of God and our relationship to God and to one another, must begin with what is happening around us. If we endeavor to attune ourselves to experiencing the world as it is, this will lead us through a process of interpreting and wrestling with reality. It is this process, done in community and by the light of Sacred Scripture and tradition, that blooms in an expansive imagination and can become effective action for the reign of God.
John Paul II wrote that “beauty will save the world”; in doing this he was echoing a long tradition uniting the aesthetic with the ethical. Sixteen years later, Pope Francis would also appeal to beauty as a powerful aid to building ecological solidarity, naming beauty and its effects over 40 times in his encyclical “Laudato Si ’.” He writes: “Faith allows us to interpret the meaning and the mysterious beauty of what is unfolding” in the universe. He adds that Jesus “was able to invite others to be attentive to the beauty that there is in the world because he himself was in constant touch with nature, lending it an attention full of fondness and wonder.” The insight into the power of beauty encouraged ancient thinkers to identify qualities they called the universals, or the transcendentals. These were ways of experiencing reality and evaluating it that appeared to be so fundamental that they were shared across radically diverse human groups. So how can we unite around these principles?
Understand what is good. Despite differences across cultures, humans seem to share some basic understanding of what is good. Religious codes throughout the world often converge in defining what is good and what is not. Ancient peoples understood that there were markers in the ways life unfolded that showed what would help a community flourish and markers that conversely cried out “caution” and pointed to what would hinder and thwart a community’s survival. Good was real and so was evil, and the difference between them needed to be understood and acted upon.
Embrace what is true. Humans also seem to share an ability to assess what is true and what is not. These assessments of truthfulness are not connected to our simplistic modern idea of “the factual” but rather to a more robust and profound experience, the experience of wisdom resonant in the human heart. There are truths and there are also lies; and as history painfully shows, the difference between these is vital to the survival of a community. This difference also needs to be visible, understood and acted upon.
Behold beauty. Beyond goodness and truth, the ancients identified a third “universal,” and some of us give it pride of place because it validates the other two by attracting us and pointing us toward them. This is what we call beauty, and unlike some who would claim “beauty is in the eye of the beholder,” reducing it to a purely subjective experience, those of us who argue for the transcendental power of beauty are closer to Shakespeare’s idea that “a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.” The sweetness is universally felt, universally recognized and universally delightful, regardless of what name we might give it. What’s more, in a Christian understanding, beauty and our ability to recognize and love it originate in God’s abundant generosity and communicate God’s presence with us. As John Paul II puts it, beauty “has drawn its sap precisely from the mystery of the Incarnation.” This was the experience my son had.
Find strength in unity. The strength of the transcendentals is precisely in their unity and how they bring us to union with a mystery that wants to be known. If something is good, then it is also true and most assuredly beautiful. And since beauty is perceptible through our senses and thus present in the world, it can do the work of revealing the other two. Nothing can be beautiful if it lies or leads us into evil. Because of this, beauty’s opposite—ugliness—is also a valuable and powerful ethical marker that we must be capable of recognizing and acting upon. What I want to highlight here is that the events of our present day reveal that we have neglected to cultivate our ability to see true beauty and consequently have become blind to its heartbreaking absence in ugliness. This failure is playing a critical role in what is happening in our world. What happens when we can no longer recognize beauty? What happens when ugliness is camouflaged so we cannot see it? What is the outcome of losing our ability to discern the true and the good?

articles.title_orig: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion-year-old millisecond signal from space
articles.title_zh: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion-year-old millisecond signal from space
articles.content_orig:
More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds.
In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age.
Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified.
We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time.
The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth.
By measuring the amount of dispersion, we can tell how much of this material the signal has passed through – which in turn lets us calculate how far the signal has travelled and how far away from us it was created.
The FRB 20240304B burst showed a large amount of dispersion, which suggested it was probably coming from a great distance. We were also able to pinpoint its position on the sky.
But when we looked at that position with large ground-based telescopes like the Keck Telescopes , we couldn’t see a host galaxy. The galaxy was simply too faint.
So we turned to the James Webb Space Telescope ( JWST ). The space telescope’s infrared camera revealed a tiny galaxy very close to the position of the fast radio burst.
We then broke down light from the galaxy into the spectrum of different frequencies that made it up. We know what part of this spectrum “should” look like, and seeing how those frequencies have changed lets us calculate how fast the galaxy is moving away from us due to the expansion of the universe – which in turn lets us figure out how old it is.
These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago.
The host galaxy itself was another surprise.
It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found.
This is consistent with one theory about the source of at least some fast radio bursts – that they are produced by young, highly magnetised neutron stars called magnetars .
At the same time, fast radio bursts come in different shapes and sizes, we don’t think all of them necessarily have the same kind of origin.
However, observations like ours give us another piece of the puzzle. By studying the host galaxies and the environments of fast radio bursts across cosmic time, we can start to understand which types of galaxies and stellar environments produce them.
The most exciting thing about this discovery, however, may not be the distance itself.
As the radio signal made its way to Earth, it picked up the imprint of everything it passed through, bearing a record of the magnetic fields, changes in the space environment, and turbulence that it encountered. This makes it a gold mine of information about the cosmos that is otherwise difficult to access.
This includes how electrons are distributed through the cosmic web, as well as information on magnetic fields that pervade the universe. As the signal encounters magnetic fields along the way they subtly twist the orientation of its radio waves. By measuring this twist, we learn about the magnetic field complexities across many billions of light years.
FRB 20240304B does more than tell us about one distant galaxy. It gives us a new data point for studying how electrically charged matter has been distributed through the universe over cosmic time, and also how magnetised the cosmos is.
Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. This lets us probe electrically charged matter across about 80% of cosmic history.
Finding fast radio bursts at such large distances is difficult because of the combination of detecting increasingly faint bursts and identifying galaxies that are themselves extremely faint.
The next step is to find many more.
With larger samples of distant fast radio bursts, we can use these brief flashes as cosmic signposts, revealing how matter is spread through the universe, how galaxies grow, and how the space between them changes over time.

Ferritin is having a moment. The iron-storage protein is showing up more and more in conversations about fatigue, wellness and blood work, but what does your ferritin number actually tell you?
Ferritin is a blood marker that gives doctors a window into how much iron is stored in the body. With recent changes to the guidelines for diagnosing iron deficiency, ferritin levels are getting even more attention.
Earlier this month, the American Society of Hematology (ASH) released new guidelines for diagnosing iron deficiency, recommending higher ferritin thresholds than have traditionally been used. The goal is to identify iron deficiency earlier, before it develops into iron deficiency anemia.
So, what does your ferritin number actually tell you? Here’s what to know.
“Ferritin is a protein that stores iron in our bodies and is a reflection of how much iron storage we have,” says Dr. Angela Weyand , a clinical professor of pediatric hematology-oncology at the University of Michigan Medical School and a member of the expert panel that established the new ASH guidelines.
Think of ferritin as your body’s iron savings account. The body stores iron so it can access it when needed. Iron is essential for making hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body. But iron also plays roles in muscle metabolism, cellular function and other processes.
Iron has many functions, but the most important is making red blood cells. When your body doesn’t have enough iron coming in or is losing more iron than it can replace, it starts drawing from iron stores. As those stores become depleted, ferritin levels fall. That’s why ferritin is an important tool for identifying iron deficiency. “The best test for most people to assess iron deficiency is ferritin,” Dr. Weyand says.
Iron deficiency is extremely common. A 2025 review in JAMA estimated that iron deficiency affects about 2 billion people worldwide and about 14% of adults in the United States.
When iron stores are depleted, the body may not have enough iron available for processes involved in energy production, muscle function and cognitive function. Some people have no obvious symptoms of iron deficiency, while others may experience fatigue, weakness, dizziness, headaches, shortness of breath, difficulty concentrating or restless leg syndrome. As iron deficiency becomes more severe and progresses to iron deficiency anemia, symptoms can become more pronounced, including fatigue, weakness, difficulty concentrating and reduced exercise or work capacity.
The important distinction is that iron deficiency and iron deficiency anemia are not the same thing. Iron deficiency can occur before anemia develops, which is one reason ferritin is useful — it can help identify depleted iron stores before the deficiency progresses further.
Iron deficiency can happen to anyone, but some people are at higher risk, including those who:
Diet can also play a role in iron stores. Plant foods including beans, lentils, tofu, nuts, seeds and fortified cereals, contain non-heme iron, which isn’t absorbed as well as the heme iron found in meat and seafood. As a result, vegetarians and vegans should eat almost twice the amount of daily iron , as compared to those who eat meat.
While diet can be one contributor to low ferritin levels, blood loss and problems with iron absorption are also common causes of iron deficiency. If a blood test shows that your ferritin is low, your health care provider can help determine what may be causing the iron deficiency and whether treatment is needed.
For years, laboratories have typically determined a “normal” ferritin range by looking at the distribution of ferritin levels in a population. But ASH says these statistical reference ranges aren’t necessarily the best way to determine when iron stores are too low.
A laboratory reference range describes what is statistically typical in a particular population. But being outside that range doesn’t necessarily mean a person has a medical condition, and being inside it doesn’t always mean there is no clinically meaningful issue.
“The recommendations changed because using reference ranges, which take a presumed healthy population and define ‘normal’ using a standard curve doesn’t work for a condition that affects so many people,” Dr. Weyand says. “The new recommendations are based on clinical outcomes and measures, rather than relying on a statistical analysis.”
She says these types of clinical outcomes are also used for other conditions that affect a large population, such as high cholesterol.
That means some people who previously received a “normal” ferritin result may now meet the criteria for iron deficiency.
The new guidelines recommend these ferritin thresholds for diagnosing iron deficiency:
Ferritin is measured through a simple blood test. If you’re experiencing symptoms that could be related to iron deficiency, have a risk factor, such as heavy menstrual bleeding or pregnancy, or have had iron deficiency in the past, ask your healthcare provider whether checking your ferritin makes sense.
And don’t be surprised if your ferritin result doesn’t come back with a simple “normal” or “abnormal” answer.
There are many factors to take into consideration when assessing ferritin status, but the new ASH recommendations are intended to help clinicians recognize iron deficiency more consistently.
If your ferritin is low, the next step is figuring out why. Treatment may involve increasing dietary iron, taking an iron supplement or addressing an underlying cause, such as blood loss or an absorption problem.
But don’t start taking high-dose iron simply because your ferritin is on the low end of normal. Too much iron can be harmful, and the appropriate treatment depends on whether you actually have iron deficiency, what’s causing it and your overall health.
If you’re concerned about your ferritin level, talk with your healthcare provider about how to interpret the result alongside your symptoms, medical history and other iron studies.
While low ferritin can be a sign of iron deficiency, a high ferritin level doesn’t necessarily mean you have too much iron.
Ferritin can increase in response to inflammation, so elevated levels can occur with acute or chronic inflammation, chronic alcohol consumption, liver disease, renal failure and metabolic syndrome. High ferritin can also have other causes, including iron overload, certain cancers or repeated blood transfusions.
That’s why an elevated ferritin result needs to be interpreted in context with your health care provider. In other words, a high ferritin number isn’t automatically a sign that you have too much iron, just as a “normal” ferritin number doesn’t always rule out iron deficiency.
Natalie Rizzo is a New York City-based dietitian, the founder of Greenletes and author of "Planted Performance."

articles.title_orig: Long-Term Care Costs: The U.S. Versus the Rest of the World
articles.title_zh: Long-Term Care Costs: The U.S. Versus the Rest of the World
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. has no unified program for long-term care, so families piece together coverage from Medicaid, private insurance, and out-of-pocket spending.
Most other countries have built dedicated long-term care systems, using approaches ranging from social insurance to means-tested safety nets.
Unpaid family caregiving remains the backbone of long-term care in every country, including those with generous public systems.
Planning ahead, including learning your state's Medicaid rules and options, is the best protection against the financial shock of long-term care.
Most of us will need help with everyday tasks later in our lives, such as bathing, dressing, cooking, and getting around. How that help gets paid, however, depends on where in the world you are.
Living a long life comes with a sobering statistic: most older adults will need some form of long-term care (LTC) before they die. LTC is different from the medical care most think of when considering services typically covered by health insurance. It might involve a home health aide who helps someone bathe and dress, an adult day program, or a room in a nursing home.
Local Elder Law Attorneys in Your City
In the U.S. it is paid for differently compared to other countries. Around the world, other wealthy countries have built national systems to help cover long-term care costs. The United States has not.
Understanding how we pay for long-term care versus citizens of other countries can help with planning for the future.
In the United States, there is no single program that automatically pays for long-term care. Instead, families rely on a patchwork of sources:
Medicare doesn’t cover it. Medicare , the federal health insurance available after 65, pays for doctors and hospital stays but not long-term care services. As such, it will not provide ongoing help with activities of daily living like bathing or eating. However, it should cover a short stay in a skilled nursing facility after a hospitalization.
Medicaid pays for more than half of LTC, but only after you’ve spent down your savings. The joint state-federal program for people with low income is the largest single payer of long-term care in the U.S. But to qualify, most people must first spend nearly all of their savings. Typically, they must have less than $2,000 or $3,000 in countable assets, with the exact rules varying by state.
Private long-term care insurance covers only a small slice. A relatively small share of Americans have private long-term care insurance. Policies have become more expensive and harder to find over the past decade. Even those with policies may find they do not fully cover the cost of care.
Families absorb the rest. Out-of-pocket spending and unpaid family caregiving fill in the gaps. Nursing home care can cost more than $100,000 a year . Family caregivers report spending roughly a quarter of their income, on average, on caregiving-related costs.
According to a 2023 Commonwealth Fund analysis , the U.S. spends less, as a percentage of their GDP, on long-term care than almost any other wealthy country — even though total U.S. health spending is far higher overall. The financial burden that remains falls hardest on women, as the largest demographic of unpaid caregivers.
Most other high-income countries built long-term care systems decades ago. Plus, they spend more on LTC relative to the size of their economies than the U.S. does. Globally, four broad approaches are most common:
Social insurance. Every worker pays into a dedicated fund, usually through payroll taxes, and becomes eligible for benefits regardless of income. Benefits may be capped and some out-of-pocket costs may apply. Germany, the Netherlands, Japan, and South Korea use this approach.
Universal, comprehensive coverage. This single-payer approach is funded through general revenues and cost sharing and is administered by a government entity. Norway and Sweden use this system.
Residual, or means-tested safety nets. This general revenue-funded system acts more as a safety net for those who can’t afford long-term care. To qualify, individuals must meet eligibility requirements and pass a means test that considers income, assets, or both. This type of system is funded through general revenues. The United Kingdom and New Zealand are examples of countries using this approach.
Hybrid approach. A combination of two or more of the above approaches. For example, France has a fragmented system that varies from national, regional, and municipal levels. Income-adjusted universal coverage for those over 60 is typically combined with supplemental private insurance. This voluntary insurance is paid by the family, with prices increasing with income.
In Canada, long-term care is not considered an insured service under the Canada Health Act . The provinces and territories use universal financing from general revenues to fund it. LTC is generally needs- and means-tested, though availability within capped budgets depends on the province or territory.
Residents in Australia must pass a needs-based test to qualify. The federal government covers the majority of the cost for those who are deemed to need it. In Switzerland, LTC costs are partially covered by compulsory health insurance. The rest is paid out-of-pocket.
Starting at age 30, workers in Singapore are automatically enrolled in CareShield Life , a mandatory long-term care insurance plan. Lower-income participants receive subsidized premiums and a separate means-tested cash grant available for caregiving costs.
More generous financing doesn’t necessarily mean long-term care is free or easily accessible in any country. Even in countries with strong public systems, roughly half of households report they cannot afford the formal long-term care they need. Unpaid family members, mostly women, still provide much of the hands-on care, often at a real cost to their own careers and finances. A more generous system reduces the financial shock but it doesn’t eliminate the caregiving burden.
Some U.S. states are experimenting with their own approaches, since there’s no comprehensive federal program on the horizon. The most prominent is Washington State’s WA Cares Fund , the first program of its kind in the country.
Several others, including California, Michigan, New York, and Minnesota, have studied similar ideas. As of now none has enacted a program as comprehensive as Washington’s.
Whatever your state does, planning ahead is the best protection against the financial shock long-term care can bring. A few starting points:
Check whether your state has its own long-term care benefit, savings program, or caregiver support fund.
Ask an elder law attorney or benefits counselor about Medicaid’s asset and income rules in your state well before you think you’ll need them. The rules and lookback periods are complex and state specific.
If you’re considering private long-term care insurance, compare policies carefully. Buy earlier rather than later, since premiums rise and health-based denials become more likely with age.
Talk with family members now about caregiving expectations and costs. Unpaid family care remains the backbone of long-term care in every country — including the ones with generous public systems.
Look into your Area Agency on Aging or state Aging and Disability Resource Center . These resources can point you toward local, low-cost, or free supports you may not know exist.

articles.title_orig: Best 50 bars in the world have been revealed – and 18 are in Europe
articles.title_zh: Best 50 bars in the world have been revealed – and 18 are in Europe
articles.content_orig:
The annual ranking of the 50 Best Bars in the world has been revealed, and 18 are in Europe.
Following its unveiling of positions 51-100 in September, the prestigious ranking body revealed that Hong Kong’s Bar Leone held on to the top spot for a second year running.
The results were announced at a ceremony in Milan on Wednesday, and two European bars – Moebius Milano in Milan and Line in Athens – featured in the top 10.
Europe was far and away the most represented continent in the ranking with its 18 spots. It also achieved a further 18 wins in the 51-100 extended list, meaning it takes up more than a third of the positions overall.
Italy had plenty to celebrate, with Moebius Milano taking second place and the top spot in Europe, while Italy’s other entry, Locale Firenze in Florence, was at number 33.
Paris has overtaken London as the most represented European city on the list for the first time, with four bars making the cut. The Cambridge Public House is number 13, followed by Bar Nouveau at 15, newcomer De Vie at 23 and Danico at 26. That puts Paris level with Hong Kong and New York as the cities with the most bars in the global top 50.
London still has a strong showing, led by Connaught Bar at number eight. Satan’s Whiskers is 29, while new entry Waltz comes in at 32.
Athens also has three bars on the list. Line leads the way at number five, while The Bar in Front of the Bar climbed 28 places to 19, earning the Nikka Highest Climber Award. Barro Negro rounds out the city’s entries at 40.
Spain has three bars in total, with Barcelona’s Sips at 16 and Paradiso at 17, while Madrid’s Angelita makes its debut at 50. Paradiso also picked up the Rémy Martin Legend of the List Award.
The top five are very varied, geographically and style-wise, and are all well worth adding to any bar lover’s bucket list.
Italian bartender Lorenzo Antinori opened this Hong Kong venue in 2023, bringing the atmosphere of a traditional Roman neighbourhood bar to the city.
The focus is on classic Italian aperitivo, with simple, well-made cocktails and a relaxed setting. Although it’s relatively new to the scene, Bar Leone has already cemented itself as something of an institution in the Asian city.
Milan’s Moebius Milano has made a significant leap up the ranking, climbing from seventh place last year to number two in 2026.
The bar is part of a much larger venue housed in a former textile factory, combining cocktails, food, music and design under one roof.
Its cocktail offering ranges from classic serves to more experimental creations, while the industrial setting gives it a distinctly contemporary Milanese feel.
Alquímico in Cartagena has taken third place, making it the highest-ranked bar outside Europe and Asia.
Set inside a restored colonial mansion in the heart of the Colombian city, the bar stretches across three floors, each with its own atmosphere and cocktail menu.
Drinks draw heavily on Colombian ingredients and landscapes, with the team using local produce and traditional techniques to create a menu that changes with the country’s seasons.
Bangkok’s Bar Us has secured fourth place, making it the Thai capital’s highest-ranked bar this year.
The intimate venue takes a tasting-menu approach to cocktails, with drinks designed around seasonal ingredients and carefully balanced flavour combinations.
Rather than simply ordering from a conventional drinks list, guests are taken through a series of serves that explore different ingredients and techniques. It’s part of Bangkok’s growing reputation as one of Asia’s major cocktail destinations.
Athens’ Line has climbed to fifth place, making it the second highest-ranked European bar on this year’s list.
Housed in one of the Greek city’s most significant former art galleries, it offers cocktails with a strong focus on fermentation.
Many of its ingredients are made in-house, including fermented fruit, syrups and other preparations used in the drinks.
The result is a menu that puts Greek produce and flavours at the centre of the experience, while the industrial-inspired setting keeps things relaxed and contemporary.

articles.title_orig: 4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space
articles.title_zh: 4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space
articles.content_orig:
NASA's Crew-12 members gather for a portrait in the pressure suits they wore while departing the International Space Station inside the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft. From left, Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, NASA astronauts Jack Hathaway and Jessica Meir, and European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot. NASA via Anil Menon hide caption
Three astronauts and a cosmonaut of NASA's Crew-12 mission have safely returned to Earth after an almost eight-month trip to the International Space Station.
The crew, commanded by NASA's Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway with mission specialists Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency and Andrey Fedyaev of Russia's Roscosmos, splashed down into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles, Calif., on Thursday, aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule.
Their trip home started about 45 minutes before, at an orbital speed of 17,500 mph.
The spacecraft lit its thrusters to nudge it out of orbit, causing the capsule to plunge into the atmosphere, its ablative heat shield battling extreme temperatures (up to 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit) during the fiery reentry. Over the course of about half an hour, the capsule slowed to a few hundred miles per hour, and then four orange-and-white parachutes took over, easing the spacecraft to just 16 mph above the cool, blue ocean and a gentle plop into the water.
The Crew-12 mission was the 20th time SpaceX had sent humans into orbit, lifting off in February on a Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida. It docked with the space station the next day . During the eight months in space, NASA said the crew completed dozens of science experiments and research, including studies of stem cells, how crystals grow in space and bone loss in microgravity.
Not all of their work happened inside the space station. Meir conducted four spacewalks totaling just over 27 hours to perform maintenance and upgrade the aging orbital outpost. Adenot performed three spacewalks.
Before departing, members of the Crew-12 mission were relieved by the three astronauts and cosmonaut of Crew-13 , who arrived at the space station last week to start a six-month rotation.
During a pre-departure news conference on the station last month, Meir said she couldn't wait to be reunited with her 3 1/2-year-old daughter.
But there was something else she missed after all this time in orbit. "So looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves. Experiencing all those things that we don't have up here," she said.
The two-time space veteran said there were two things she'd miss about space: weightlessness and the wonderful views of Earth.

articles.title_orig: ‘The Floating World’ by Ben Eastham, Reviewed
articles.title_zh: ‘The Floating World’ by Ben Eastham, Reviewed
articles.content_orig:
For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, the art critic’s debut novel remains surprisingly sincere about art itself
The unnamed narrator of Ben Eastham’s debut novel, The Floating World , is, like Eastham himself , an art critic. Grieving his recently deceased wife, he feels lost while teaching at a school where the students refer to him as ‘Doctor Pissington’. Then a friend offers him a job back in the artworld. He is to work on ‘The Floating World’, which is ‘a gated community beneath a giant dome on a desert island’ being built by a tech billionaire for the wealthiest as a refuge from climate crisis and political collapse. Our morally conflicted protagonist is hired to conduct research for an art exhibition marking the island’s inauguration. The novel negotiates the contradiction of inhabiting a contemporary artworld sustained by the good intentions of art workers who align themselves with beauty and virtue, while depending on the very forces their work purports to resist.
It opens with the narrator, in Ireland, on the verge of writing, before disappearing into his recollections, and eventually returns to the point at which the story is being written (more on which later). Grief provides its emotional landscape: the narrator’s reality is shot through with the frenetic despair that comes with the sudden loss of his wife. His grief gradually becomes entangled with the project of ‘The Floating World’ and the people making it, forcing a confrontation with the loss he has been carrying. It is in such experiences that resist ordinary expression that art becomes most meaningful: a painting, for example, that is ‘a truth that didn’t need explaining. No aristocrats, no symbolism, no lies. A painting clear as love’; and another, when the narrator’s friend likens the experience of pregnancy to a painting they once saw in a museum, in which ‘The colours are stronger and brighter, there’s a texture. It’s like breaking through a screen, the world feels bigger, like it can’t be contained.’
Eastham is at his most sensitive when criticism itself becomes inadequate. There is a pleasing irony in an art critic writing about an art critic for whom, and for the artists around him, the most profound encounters with art seem to occur precisely when interpretation fails. While Eastham is tender in his descriptions of art, his acute observations of the people surrounding it can be lacerating. He has a formidable talent for summoning up a character – or skewering one – in a sentence. One woman possesses ‘the erotic hauteur of an academic who in her youth danced beneath filtered spotlights at psychedelic happenings’. Another, ‘a woman in those oversized metal-rimmed spectacles designed to signal to civilians that the wearer is an intellectual’. Eastham is exacting not only when it comes to how people appear, but also about the identities they are trying, sometimes desperately, to project. Despite the grieving anguish of its narrator, it is his wry, deadpan humour that carries the novel. There is a dryly comic sparring match with a ‘philanthropist’ who believes happiness can be quantified, and a conversation between partygoers about where, literally, ‘the shit is going’. At times it is not unlike a drawing-room comedy, with its sharp wit, back-and-forth banter and clever insults.
The metafictional frame allows the novel to avoid the aftermath of its most dramatic events, dwelling instead on the act of remembering and reconstructing them. I’m not convinced this framing adds to the reader’s understanding of the narrator’s grief or the events being recounted. The narrator returns to remarkably similar emotional terrain at the end: melancholic and still lost, but perhaps slightly more hopeful for the future. For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, The Floating World remains surprisingly sincere about art itself. This is especially persuasive when Eastham uses art to give shape to experiences that elude explanation – love, pregnancy, grief – reminding us that beneath the bullshit posturing of the artworld is an unexpectedly earnest faith that art can make felt what we cannot quite articulate.
The Floating World by Ben Eastham. Fitzcarraldo Editions , £14.99 (softcover)

articles.title_orig: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.title_zh: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.content_orig:
Families today are âa challenging mosaic of diverse realities, marked by joys, hopes, struggles and wounds. The family is not only a place to which the Church brings the Gospel. It is also a place from which the Gospel comes alive â from one generation to another, from one family to another, and from families to society.â
Cardinal Filipe Neri Ferrão, Metropolitan Archbishop of Goa and Daman, opened his address with this reflection at the start of the second day of Pope Leo XIVâs meeting with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Bishopsâ Conferences, ten years after Amoris laetitia .
The Indian Cardinal addressed the theme âFamilies today: reality, beauty and challenges. Discerning the signs of the times through the experience of families and the Churchâs pastoral commitment today.â
He invited participants in the meeting, conducted in a synodal style, to ask themselves in their discernment: âWhat is the Holy Spirit asking the Church to change?â
This concerned ânot only in what we do for the families, but in how we understand, accompany and empower them as protagonists of the Gospel and as enduring loci of Godâs revelation.â
Drawing on his experience as a pastor in Asia, particularly in India, Cardinal Neri Ferrão acknowledged that families had changed in their identity, nature, and composition, with smaller households, new forms of cohabitation, and interreligious marriages.
Families were increasingly on the move, and many faced economic insecurity, poverty, unemployment, and uncertainty about the future.
âChristian families in many parts of India and Asia,â the Cardinal stressed, âmust also live amid growing religious polarisation and hostility, making the public expression and transmission of faith increasingly difficult.â
Yet, these families also offered the Church beauty through their care for children, the elderly, the sick, and vulnerable people. Even amid poverty and uncertainty, the Cardinal explained, âour families continue to create positive spaces for joy and hope.â
Following the publication of Amoris laetitia , he recalled, the Churches in India and across Asia âlistened first to families,â and that listening âshaped how we walk with them. We now see marriage preparation as the start of a lifelong journey, offer spiritual renewal and counselling to couples and children, and keep forming families and lay leaders over time.â
He stressed that pastoral ministry needed to move âfrom mission to families to mission among families.â Families were not simply recipients of assistance but, in his words, âthe Church's partners in mission.â
Cardinal Neri Ferrão concluded by recounting the experience of a priest who had begun family ministry in his parish not with a program, but by visiting a family experiencing underlying difficulties in communication between the parents and between them and their children. It had begun with âa conversation and a willingness to listen.â
The second speaker, Vincenzo Rosito, Professor of the History and Culture of Family Institutions at the Pontifical Lateran University and Vice Dean of the Pontifical John Paul II Theological Institute for Marriage and Family Sciences, summed up his address with questions to guide participantsâ synodal discernment.
He began with an invitation inspired by Pope Leo XIVâs reflections in the encyclical Magnifica humanitas : âLet each of us be mindful of the relationships we build within our own families and within the Church.â
Professor Rosito stressed that âfamily practices, in fact, help us to understand how churches and families learn from one another. Both the Church and the family, in fact, learn through the practices of their daily lives.â
He then offered a question for participants to consider as a father, mother, theologian, or pastor: âAm I able to recognise and share with others at least one new thing that I have learnt to do, or to do differently, in recent years of my family or pastoral life?â
Changes in family life, Prof. Rosito explained, âare not problemsâ but âhuman activities.â Recalling Amoris laetitia , he presented them as an opportunity, as concrete processes âin which individuals and families act, react, learn and develop new resources.â
âConsider, for example,â the political philosopher continued, âhow the use of new digital technologies is transforming the daily habits of families and the way children are brought up.â
The family and the Church, Prof. Rosito continued, âlearn together through change.â He drew on the Gospel image of Jesus, Joseph, and Maryâs flight into Egypt.
He noted that today, âdrawing on the experiences of refugee and migrant families, some Christian communities are re-establishing themselves as ârefuge churchesââ for those arriving in a new land or making a long journey.
He also addressed the tragedy of violence shared by many families: âThe insecurity stemming from social and political violence is a worrying reality that many Churches must deal with today, in their daily lives.â Such insecurity, he warned, could âeven devour family bonds and church relationships themselves.â
Josephâs dream was also part of the experience of this flight.
âTo dream, to imagine new forms for the Church,â Prof. Rosito concluded, âalso means renewing what we already do. To imagine the Church means being willing to learn from one another, whilst we are transformed together, as churches and as families.â
His final question for discernment was therefore: âWhat do we need, amidst the light and shadow of today, to learn and imagine new ways of being a family and new ways of being the Church?â

articles.title_orig: Amazon launches first Android tablets, raising prices and incorporating Alexa
articles.title_zh: Amazon launches first Android tablets, raising prices and incorporating Alexa
articles.content_orig:
Amazon on Thursday debuted a set of new, pricier Alexa tablets and said it's ditching its budget-friendly Fire lineup, marking a significant shift in the e-commerce juggernaut's devices strategy.
The company unveiled 8-inch, 11-inch and 12-inch models, which start at $230 and run up to $550. All devices are available for preorder on Thursday and will begin shipping Oct. 14.
Amazon has historically sold its devices at or near the cost of manufacturing them, partly to undercut competitors with extremely cheap prices, but also with the goal of promoting its other products and services. It's hoped that for every $80 Echo smart speaker it sells, users will purchase movies, audiobook subscriptions or items from its sprawling webstore, which tend to have higher margins.
The company has recently taken steps to make more money from its devices business under CEO Andy Jassy , who succeeded founder Jeff Bezos in 2021. Last year, it introduced pricier versions of its Echo smart speakers and began charging non-Prime members a subscription for Alexa+ , the souped-up version of its digital assistant.
The $550 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs more than double the price of the $155 Fire HD 10, Amazon's base model, and puts it more in line with Apple 's iPad, which runs from $449 to $1,199.
The launch comes as Amazon and other device makers are grappling with a historic surge in memory prices . Amazon in August boosted prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs and other hardware, citing the memory crunch. And earlier this year, Apple raised its prices on MacBooks and iPads, while Nintendo hiked the price of its Switch 2 console.
Amazon denied that rising memory costs played a role in its decision to charge more for the Alexa tablet. But Panos Panay, the company's devices boss, acknowledged that the shortage made it "quite tricky" to build a premium tablet at a reasonable price without making any "trade-offs."
"I think the team did a good job designing without making that trade," Panay told CNBC in an interview. "They gave you the full craftsmanship of a product, but are able to keep it at that price point."
The company said the Alexa tablet's improved speed and performance, artificial intelligence features, and upgraded design warrant a higher price tag and put the devices on par with "the best tablets on the market."
Amazon added a sleeker, sturdier aluminum backing, higher resolution display and faster processors. On the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, the highest-end model, it incorporated "Nanomatte" display technology that was developed in partnership with Corning to "dramatically reduce screen glare."
One of the most notable upgrades is that all of the devices run Google 's Android operating system, a major departure from earlier models, which relied on a custom Android version dubbed Fire OS and used Amazon's own app store, limiting the number of apps that were available.
It's also the first time Amazon has attached a set of devices to the Alexa brand, the company's automated assistant first launched in 2014 via the Echo smart speaker. Alexa is front and center in the new tablets, via a "dynamic tab" on the home screen that offers recommendations and lets users quickly pick up where they left off reading or watching a TV show. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to ask questions.
The company also introduced a new feature called "On-Screen Intelligence," where users can ask Alexa to look at what's on their screen and make suggestions or take actions.
In a demo, Panay showed how users could watch a TikTok clip of someone cooking on a grill and ask Alexa to shop for a burger press used in the video. Users can also pull up a game schedule and add every date to their calendar, Amazon said.
"She'll do the homework, and if things work out, she's going to bring up a shopping list where I can just hit buy now," Panay said.
Amazon said it will continue to support the Fire lineup for four years after the final shipment and consumers can continue using their devices as they do today, but it is no longer manufacturing new units. The Fire lineup includes a 10-inch and 8-inch model as well as two versions targeted for kids.

articles.title_orig: NASA photo of Mars dawn reveals cliffs in unprecedented detail
articles.title_zh: NASA photo of Mars dawn reveals cliffs in unprecedented detail
articles.content_orig:
The captivating shapes of wind-carved crags called yardangs are revealed in this zoomed-in crop of a broader panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover on Aug. 11, 2026. Scientists are eager to learn more about how the yardang layer formed.
Sunlight illuminates wind-carved cliffs in a dramatic new image.
A newly released panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity rover offers the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission’s scientists have long been waiting to see up close. The scene was snapped at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, showing striking blue hues in the foreground as bright morning light illuminates crags known as yardangs on the horizon.
The panorama was captured by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission, and comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth. Unlike most of Curiosity’s Mastcam images, this one was processed without white balancing, preserving the early morning appearance.
The six shots that make up this panorama, captured by NASA’s Curiosity on Aug. 11, were stitched together after being sent back to Earth. Unlike most images from the rover’s Mastcam, this one was processed without the usual white balancing — an artistic choice that preserves the early morning appearance.
The yardang layer extends roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. In fact, the rover recently passed another milestone in its ascent, reaching 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) of elevation — the most ever climbed on Mars. As it draws ever-closer to the yardangs, mission scientists expect to get even more amazing imagery — and, they hope, answers to how these cliffs were created.
Mount Sharp is made up of layers, each recording a distinct period of Mars’ history. By studying them, scientists have been able to learn more about lakes and streams that covered this part of the Red Planet billions of years ago. Eventually, the water dried up and left salty minerals behind. After new material stopped settling on the mountain, some of it may have been stripped away by wind, giving rise to the yardangs.
This artist’s concept shows Mount Sharp, the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that NASA’s Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. The location of the yardang layer, which the rover recently captured from a distance, is indicated by an ellipse annotation on the mountain’s northwestern shoulder.
NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this view looking back at the floor of Gale Crater on Sept. 5, 2026. Just nine days prior, the rover had marked 1 kilometer of elevation gain above the crater floor since beginning its ascent of Mount Sharp in 2014.
“The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.”
Curiosity is in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which started with an exploration of the spiderweb-like boxwork ridges . The rover will spend most of the next year or so driving through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying on the surface. Sometime in 2027, scientists hope to reach the base of the yardangs, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect one-of-a-kind data on these mysterious features.
