articles.title_orig: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
articles.title_zh: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles in Gulf off Qatar, maritime agency says
articles.content_orig:
A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
The incident - a rare attack deep inside the Gulf - happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal with casualties reported, the UKMTO said.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers. On Saturday it was reported as sailing towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).
The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.
This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.
Also on Thursday, Vanguard amended an earlier report that had said there was a fire on board another tanker in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.
The company clarified that there were no indications a fire occurred on the vessel, which it had identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

articles.title_orig: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
articles.title_zh: A hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
articles.content_orig:
The global energy system is already being pushed to the brink. A hurricane barreling down on America’s refining nerve center is the last thing that’s needed.
Isaias, the Atlantic season’s first hurricane , is arriving at a time when there is almost no margin for error.
US refineries, mostly located along the Gulf Coast, are running as hard as they can to offset war-driven outages overseas. Fuel inventories that act as shock absorbers have already been tapped. And America’s emergency oil stockpile is at the lowest level since 1982.
Hurricane Isaias “could be a gigantic event. It’s the worst time something like this could happen in 25 years,” said Robert Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho Securities.
The actual impact of Isaias will depend on the storm’s path and intensity.
Current forecasts call for the storm to hit east of New Orleans, a major refining hub, which should spare vital energy infrastructure from the storm’s worst.
Still, major oil producers including Shell, Chevron and BP have evacuated non-essential personnel from oil platforms in the Gulf and curtailed production .
As of midday Thursday, about 1.3 million barrels per day of Gulf of Mexico oil production had been shut in, according to the federal agency Marine Minerals Administration.
That amounts to about 63% of the region’s production. And about 57% of current natural gas production in the Gulf of Mexico has been sidelined.
The risk is that the storm’s damage could squeeze supply chains even more, further raising historically high prices.
The Iran war, combined with Ukrainian drone attacks in Russia and export restrictions in China, have catapulted diesel prices to all-time highs. Gasoline was more than $4.40 per gallon last week and has never been this expensive at this time of year.
How gas station owners set their prices
About 2.7 million barrels per day, or 14%, of America’s refining capacity, lie within or near the projected of the path of the storm, according to Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.
Lipow said he expects at least some refineries in the New Orleans/Baton Rouge and Mississippi/Alabama regions will have to slow down how much oil they turn into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
Tankers delivering oil to refineries and loading fuel out of refineries could get delayed as well. This would particularly impact Florida because the state relies on shipments of fuel from the Gulf Coast.
“There is no slack in the system to make up for lost refinery capacity. Lost production will have to come out of already low commercial inventories,” Lipow wrote in an email.
Those commercial inventories have been whittled away.
Gasoline stockpiles recently fell to their lowest seasonal record since 2012, according to federal data.
Distillate inventories, which include mostly diesel, are at their lowest level for early October since tracking started in the early 1980s.
Not only that, but the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has been aggressively drained to ease the energy shock. The SPR now holds about 283 million barrels of crude, the least since 1982 when the emergency reserve was being filled during the Reagan administration.
Refineries in the Middle East have been damaged by the Iran war, or have struggled to get shipments out to the rest of the world. Refineries in Russia have been destroyed or damaged by drone attacks. And China, seeking to avoid fuel shortages, has restricted its exports.
US refineries, operating at about 95% of their capacity, are one of the remaining key sources for the global fuel supply.
“It would be a disaster if US refining capacity has to come off the market. It would basically force a diesel export ban,” said Yawger, the Mizuho executive, who added that he is not in favor of restricting US diesel exports .
Much depends on the intensity of the storm, including the severity of flooding and wind damage. Isaias could peak as a Category 2 storm with 110 mph winds by early Friday, but is expected to weaken somewhat before landfall.
Even with a Category 1 hurricane, it can take a week to return refining operations to normal.

articles.title_orig: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
articles.title_zh: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
articles.content_orig:
English English (pdf) Swedish Swedish (pdf)
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 to
Francis Halzen University of Wisconsin–Madison, USA
“for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”
Francis Halzen realised that ice at the South Pole could be used to track particles known as neutrinos. His vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors. Using IceCube, researchers can capture neutrinos from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe.
Neutrinos are everywhere, but they do not make themselves known. They pass all the way through the Earth and through our bodies without us noticing. Very rarely, a single neutrino will interact with an atomic nucleus, which makes it possible for someone with the right equipment to discover them.
Scientists have long known that the cosmos contains natural particle accelerators, which fire out particles with energies up to a million times more than can be achieved in laboratories on Earth. Much about these sources is mysterious: what are they, where are they, and what are the main processes inside them?
Neutrinos with extremely high energies are created in the same environments as other types of particles. However, unlike other particles, neutrinos reach us without changing direction or losing energy. This means they can provide information that is not available in any other way.
Francis Halzen first presented his vision for capturing neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988. When a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus, it produces a flash of light that can be tracked by sensors in the clear glacial ice. The South Pole’s ice has many advantages, as it is free from various types of interference and the area is geologically stable, with no earthquakes. Halzen and his idea soon gained the support of other researchers and, just a few years later, preliminary testing was conducted on sensors in ice.
Cosmic neutrinos with extremely high energies are very rare, so an enormous volume of ice is needed to observe an adequate number of collisions. IceCube covers an entire cubic kilometre and was finished in 2011. Researchers soon discovered the first high-energy neutrinos and, a few years later, could publish their discovery of neutrinos that must originate far outside our solar system. The search for the universe’s neutrino sources could begin in earnest.
“Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument. His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy,” says Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.
The neutrino interactions that are continuously collected by IceCube will provide researchers with novel knowledge about the violent settings in which high-energy neutrinos can be created – and could even reveal previously unknown cosmic phenomena.
